title: SLICE: one declaration set drives the key, the preview, and the agent
description:
THE COHERENCE PROOF, at the smallest size that demonstrates it.

The claim is that human, desktop and agent operate from one model. The sharpest demonstration is a
minimal CANONICAL DECLARATION SET that simultaneously produces the LIVE KEY BINDING, the SHORTCUT
PREVIEW ROW, and the AGENT-READABLE ACTION. If those three can disagree there is no shared model.

A DECLARATION SET, NOT ONE OBJECT. Three distinct declarations — one role, one action, one key
binding — kept separate because bru.7 defines them as separate registries. The slice must not
accidentally establish a permanent combined schema. Treat the file layout as provisional and expect
bru.7 to move it.

  role     mail = proton-mail
  action   desktop.application.ensure
  binding  SUPER + M -> desktop.application.ensure, role = mail

CHORD: SUPER + M, verified unbound 2026-09-02. SUPER + E was the original proposal and is WRONG:
binds.lua line 72 binds it to the file manager. Deliberately redefining a vendor chord is a
legitimate experiment about ownership, but it should be chosen, approved and recorded — not
stumbled into on the first slice. Plain SUPER letters currently free: B G H I K M N O R U Y. Note
SUPER + K is free, which the eventual shortcut preview may want.

ENSURE, NOT OPEN OR FOCUS. Open and focus differ when the application is not running, and the
original wording used both. The action is desktop.application.ensure, and its proposal must state
which branch it will take:

  running      focus window <address>
  not running  launch role mail, wait for its window, then focus it

THE SAME ACTION DOES NOT REQUIRE THE SAME INTERACTION. A person pressing a key has already
expressed immediate intent; making them approve a proposal afterwards would make the shortcut
unpleasant and would confuse one vocabulary with one interaction flow.

  human keypress  act directly
  agent request   propose, then act on approval

Action identity and implementation are shared. Authorization context differs by caller. Say so in
the design, because it is the distinction that keeps a shared vocabulary from becoming a shared
ceremony.

VENDOR BINDINGS: one explicitly observed vendor binding is enough here — SUPER + E to the file
manager is the natural choice, since it is the chord this slice deliberately avoided. Authoritative
enumeration of all 75 belongs to bru.7.

THEME IS OUT OF THIS SLICE BUT NOT OUT OF THE SYSTEM. Noctalia is the existing theme authority.
Version one verifies and references that cohesion rather than rebuilding it.

GROUNDED FACTS: hyprctl -j clients returns address, stableId, class, initialClass, title, pid,
workspace and monitor per window; Proton Mail resolved by class on 2026-09-02. binds.lua declares
75 bindings and is byte-identical to the CachyOS template, so every existing binding is
vendor-owned.
acceptance_criteria:
- Three declarations exist — role, action, key binding — as separate objects, not one combined schema.
- The live Hyprland binding, the preview row, and the agent-readable action all derive from them.
- Changing a declaration changes all three, verified by changing one.
- SUPER + M is confirmed unbound before use; SUPER + E is listed in the preview as an observed vendor binding.
- desktop.application.ensure proposes the branch it will take, distinguishing running from not running.
- A human keypress acts directly; an agent request proposes first. Both resolve to the same action identity.
- An agent ensures mail by role, without touching hyprctl or naming an executable.
- One provenance record per invocation, naming action, caller, inputs, outcome.
- Recorded judgement: does the desktop tell one truth, and where does it still not.
notes:
REVIEW APPLIED 2026-09-02, four corrections, all accepted.

1. SUPER + E collides. Verified: binds.lua line 72 binds it to the file manager. Changed to
   SUPER + M, verified unbound. Free plain SUPER letters recorded for later choices.
2. Open versus focus disagreed. The action is now desktop.application.ensure and its proposal must
   state which branch it takes.
3. Same action does not require the same interaction. Keypress acts directly, agent proposes.
   Shared identity, caller-sensitive authorization.
4. Declaration SET, not one declaration. Three separate objects, provisional layout, so the slice
   cannot pre-empt bru.7's registry boundaries.

Plus: one observed vendor binding is enough, enumeration belongs to bru.7; and theme is out of the
slice but not out of the system — Noctalia is the theme authority and version one references it.

BUILT 2026-09-02. bin/cap, 348 lines, stdlib only, peer to bin/ms.

THE COHERENCE CLAIM HOLDS, verified by changing declarations rather than by inspection:
  changing the BINDING declaration changed the live key and the preview row together
  changing the ACTION declaration changed the preview label and the agent listing together
Each declaration drives the surfaces that name it, and no surface has a second source.

WHAT EXISTS: canonical/roles/roles.toml, canonical/actions/desktop.toml and
canonical/bindings/keys.toml as three separate objects; cap list --json, propose, act, preview,
check and render; window resolution by role over hyprctl -j clients; one provenance record per
invocation carrying action, caller, phase, inputs, outcome and the plan.

THE SAFEGUARD IS A CHECK, NOT AN ASSUMPTION. cap check re-reads binds.lua every time and never
trusts a prior observation, because a CachyOS update can claim a chord. cap render REFUSES while a
declared chord conflicts. Both conflict kinds are proven able to fail: SUPER + E reports the file
manager, and two declarations on one chord report each other. The self-conflict case was originally
a no-op loop left in the code — an unfinished intent that would have passed silently.

CALLER-SENSITIVE AUTHORIZATION IS REAL, not just designed: the rendered Hyprland binding invokes
cap act with CAP_CALLER=keypress, so a person pressing the key acts directly, while an agent
proposes first. Both resolve to the same action identity and the same implementation, and the
provenance record names which caller it was.

WHERE THE DESKTOP STILL DOES NOT TELL ONE TRUTH, recorded honestly:
  - the preview shows vendor rows with their raw Lua body where a human label belongs; the
    compositor's config carries no labels to read, so 75 of 76 rows are less legible than ours
  - consequence = adjust is declared and nothing enforces it; enforcement is deferred phase 5
  - cap render and ms project are two steps, so canonical can lead the machine — ms propose reports
    it, but nothing prevents forgetting
  - roles resolve by window class only; stableId and pid are available and unused
  - one action, one role, one binding. The claim is proven at n=1 and nothing about n=20 is known.

JUDGEMENT ON THE ORIGINAL QUESTION — does this feel like operating the machine rather than
instructing a script: partly. Asking for the mail role and getting a branch-aware proposal does. The
two-step render-then-project does not; it feels like a build system, and if that friction survives
contact it is the first thing to fix.
close_reason: Coherence proven at n=1, verified by changing declarations rather than inspecting code: the binding declaration drives the live key and the preview together; the action declaration drives the preview label and the agent listing together. SUPER+M is live. Both conflict kinds proven able to fail, one of which was a no-op loop that would have passed silently. Caller-sensitive authorization implemented, not merely designed. Five remaining inconsistencies recorded in the notes rather than closed over.

title: Agent-first workstation: make the desktop operable by asking
description:
A namespaced, self-describing capability surface over the control surfaces this machine already has, with authorization metadata and provenance that none of them carry.

SEPARATE FROM ms, PERMANENTLY. ms governs durable projection and drift. This governs runtime capabilities and actions. Folding them gives the projector a runtime and the runtime the projector's write access. See CAPABILITIES.md section 1.

WHAT OMARCHY CONTRIBUTES, established by reading its manual rather than recalling it: a hierarchical command tree (omarchy GROUP COMMAND), --help at every level, a machine-readable catalogue via omarchy commands --json, and a menu that is the same tree with dotted deep-links. That architecture is worth adopting.

WHAT IT DOES NOT HAVE: an event model. Its agent integration is agent-invokes-commands. Its single reactive path, crash detection, routes through a notification a human clicks. Its authorization is auto-approving modes scoped by directory, which machine-state-yxb explicitly lists as an idea not to inherit. So the event stream and the authorization model are ours to add, and are the actual contribution.

THE SIMPLIFICATION THIS BUYS: if the command surface is self-describing and JSON-enumerable, a capability IS a command in the catalogue. The separate capability manifest sketched in CAPABILITIES.md section 3 collapses into annotations on commands.

EXISTING SURFACES ARE WRAPPED AND NORMALIZED, NEVER REPLACED: hyprctl 56 commands, noctalia msg 112, bd 114, dcg 25, ms 5.
design:
THE CENTRAL CLAIM, and the only thing version one must prove:

  The human, desktop, and agent all operate from the same model of the machine.

Not lots of AI features. Not broad application support. A small part of the workstation made
unmistakably coherent, where every surface tells the same truth.

THE PRODUCT TEST. Version one succeeds if these are true:
  - the desktop never documents a shortcut separately from defining it
  - a theme change is made once and appears consistently
  - applications are addressed by role, not by executable
  - humans and agents use the same named actions
  - the agent understands the desktop without screenshots or command guessing
  - every mutation is proposed, authorized and attributable
  - one real OS event produces genuinely useful agent assistance
  - REMOVING THE AGENT STILL LEAVES A COHERENT, FULLY USABLE WORKSTATION

That last one is the discipline. Agent-first means the machine is arranged to collaborate with
agents, not that ordinary operation collapses when a model provider is unavailable.

FOUR CANONICAL REGISTRIES: theme, applications by role, actions, and bindings. From these the
system derives Hyprland bindings, the shortcut preview, Noctalia menu entries, agent-readable
capability descriptions, and window matching.

WHAT THIS EPIC GOT WRONG TWICE, recorded so it is not repeated. First it was bottom-up: registry,
schema, loader, catalogue, contract, provider — eleven beads before anything did anything. The
correction to a single deep capability was also wrong, in a subtler way: the claim above is about
coherence ACROSS dimensions, so proving one dimension deeply proves nothing. The slice must touch
every dimension thinly instead.

THEME IS ALREADY SOLVED AND IS OUT OF SCOPE, established 2026-09-02. Noctalia is already the
semantic theme registry: config.toml declares builtin_ids of btop, gtk3, gtk4, kcolorscheme, kitty,
qt and alacritty; wallpaper_scheme is m3-tonal-spot, a semantic scheme rather than a palette copy;
54 community templates act as adapters; and noctalia msg exposes color-scheme-set and
theme-mode-set at runtime. Seven applications are themed and six have live files. A canonical
semantic theme would reimplement a working system in order to own it. Cohesion here means
REFERENCING Noctalia — recording it and exposing its runtime commands as capabilities — not
replacing it. See machine-state-a22.
acceptance_criteria: Each phase is useful on its own, attended, before the next begins. Grants go live last.
notes:
WORK BREAKDOWN COMPLETE 2026-09-02. 26 task beads across five phases, each written to be workable
by an agent holding this repository and nothing else — no memory of the conversation that produced
them. Every bead carries the shared constraints, the verified facts specific to it, and acceptance
criteria.

STRUCTURE: each phase has implementation beads, one TEST bead, and one EVAL bead. The distinction
is deliberate. A test is mechanical and deterministic and asks whether the thing works as designed.
An eval asks whether an agent actually behaves correctly when given it — which unit tests cannot
answer, because the JSON catalogue and the capability descriptions are an interface to a language
model. If agents consistently choose wrong from the catalogue, the catalogue is at fault, not the
agent, and only an eval will tell you that.

DEPENDENCY GRAPH ENCODES HARD BLOCKERS ONLY, not preferred sequence. The first attempt chained the
phases and made every child inherit the chain through its parent, leaving exactly one startable
bead out of 26 — which defeats the purpose. Phase ordering remains the recorded intent in this
epic's design field, where it belongs. What blocks is only what genuinely cannot proceed: a loader
needs a schema, a test needs the thing it tests, bindings need a catalogue to bind to.

Seven beads are startable in parallel: the skeleton and schema decisions, window resolution, the
provenance record shape, and the event envelope. Those are design and prototype work that needs
nothing built first.

VERIFIED FACTS EMBEDDED so no bead requires rediscovery: hyprctl -j clients fields and that Proton
Mail was resolvable by class; the Hyprland socket path, wire format and that the stdlib alone read
40 events in nine seconds; the D-Bus services present on each bus; that Linger is off so user timers
only fire inside a login session; the grants path and why root is the only real boundary here; and
the two known-possible authority bypasses that the adversarial eval must probe.

DESIGN REVIEW RECEIVED 2026-09-02, machine-state-bru.md at repository root, written by another
model against this epic. Its central claim is accepted: bru is not defective, but an adjacent layer
is missing — experience cohesion, meaning one semantic theme, one keybinding registry, one action
vocabulary, one application-role registry, and one account of what is ours versus a vendor's.

ACCEPTED, AND THE REASONING IS SOUND. Cohesion spans durable state and runtime action, while the
broker is deliberately runtime-only. Making the broker own themes or generate Hyprland
configuration would violate exactly the separation that keeps it out of ms. So it belongs in a
sibling epic whose declarations are canonical state projected by ms, referencing capability names
owned by bru. Reference in one direction, ownership in neither — the same shape as information may
flow up from canonical while authority may not.

ACTED ON IMMEDIATELY: the review's sharpest catch is that binding is ambiguous. bru.4.4 renamed to
event binding, reserving key binding for the cohesion layer.

QUALIFICATION THE REVIEW DOES NOT MAKE, and it is the most concrete risk in the document. Section 5
proposes a canonical semantic theme projected into applications, and section 8 argues the theme
registry can deliver value before the broker exists. But Noctalia ALREADY owns cross-application
theming on this machine: 54 templates, most with an executable apply.sh, with theme files live in
alacritty, kitty, btop, gtk-3.0, gtk-4.0 and qt6ct. A canonical theme projecting into those apps
would start a rewrite war with a running theming engine, over settings nobody here has an opinion
about. machine-state-a22 is open precisely to decide Noctalia's status FIRST, and any theme work
is blocked behind it.

SECOND QUALIFICATION, grounded 2026-09-02: binds.lua declares 75 bindings and is byte-identical to
the CachyOS template. Zero are ours. So a keybinding registry would begin by DESCRIBING vendor state
rather than owning it, and the review's observed category is not an edge case but almost the whole
initial population. That matches the pattern everywhere else here — two lines of a thousand were
ours in Hyprland, none at all in CLAUDE.md. The registry earns its keep as an accurate account of a
keymap we mostly do not own, which is a different and more modest claim than generating one.

THIRD: sequencing. The review sketches a seven-phase cohesion epic. Combined with this epic's five
phases and 26 beads, that is a great deal of plan for a repository holding 47 lines of authored
decision. Cohesion should wait until bru phases 1 and 2 have proved the vocabulary, because
otherwise it would be planned against capability identifiers that do not yet exist.

INTENT RESTATED 2026-09-02, because the plan had lost it under supporting concerns.

THE INTENT: you should be able to tell an agent what you want your desktop to do and have it
happen — through a path that is discoverable, bounded and recorded, rather than through a guessed
shell command. That is the whole of it. Everything in this epic either serves that sentence or
should be cut.

WHAT WENT WRONG WITH THE PLAN: 26 beads across five phases, correctly reasoned and entirely
bottom-up. Registry, then schema, then loader, then catalogue, then contract, then a provider —
eleven beads before anything does anything. No vertical slice, so no result until most of the plan
is built, and no way to learn the design is wrong until it is expensive to change. Written against
a repository holding 47 lines of authored decision, alongside a 255-line design document and a
308-line review.

THE CORRECTION: machine-state-bru.6 is now first and blocks every phase. It is the smallest thing
that proves the intent — focus the mail window by asking — and it deliberately builds none of the
schema, events, grants or enforcement that the phases describe.

The five phases are now explicitly WIDENING, not construction. They should be re-scoped after the
slice, not before, because the slice will show which of them are needed in the form they are
currently written. Several probably are not.

THE MEASURE IS NOT CORRECTNESS. The slice passes when asking an agent to focus a window feels like
operating the machine rather than instructing a script. If it does not feel that way, the design is
wrong and 26 beads of correct-looking plan will not save it.

PLAN REVISED TO THE INTENT 2026-09-02. Everything not serving the coherence claim is deferred, not
deleted.

IN SCOPE, because each maps to a line of the product test:
  bru.6  the slice — one declaration drives the key, the preview and the agent
  bru.7  registries: roles, actions, key bindings, and the preview derived from them
  bru.1  the action listing and the query/propose/act contract
  bru.2  desktop provider: window resolution, so the agent never guesses a title
  bru.3  provenance, so every mutation is attributable
  bru.4  ONE reactive path, rescoped from event sources generally to crash diagnosis

DEFERRED, seven beads:
  bru.5 and all three children — unattended operation and grant enforcement. The intent is explicit
    that version one needs trustworthy ATTENDED operation and read-only reactive reports, not
    sophisticated grants. The boundary already exists and ms status already verifies it.
  bru.3.4 — learning from the corpus. Version one needs the record complete, not yet analysed.
  bru.4.2 — Hyprland as an event source. The one reactive path comes from systemd-coredump; window
    queries do not need the event socket.
  bru.4.6 — follows the event work it evaluates.

FOLDED BACK IN: machine-state-1qs, the cohesion sibling epic, is closed and became bru.7. Deferring
it was wrong, because the claim version one must prove IS cohesion. A capability layer with no
shared vocabulary would satisfy none of the product test.

EXCLUDED ON EVIDENCE RATHER THAN SCOPE: theme. Noctalia already is the semantic theme registry.

THE SHAPE NOW: exactly one bead is startable, bru.6. Everything else is blocked behind it, because
the slice decides whether the remaining phases are needed in the form they are written.

title: Establish file ownership classes; verify bd's rewrite behaviour
description:
Why: provenance check (2026-08-31) disproves the premise of the previous reconciliation plan.

EVIDENCE:
- git log --follow: CLAUDE.md and AGENTS.md were both created by a single commit, 4d81b55 'bd init: initialize beads issue tracking', alongside 16 other files (.agents/, .claude/, .codex/, .beads/).
- Both are byte-identical to that commit today. Neither has ever been hand-edited. Zero human-authored lines.
- 'bd setup --list' shows 13 built-in recipes; these files are recipe OUTPUT.
- 'bd setup claude --check' reports CLAUDE.md as 'installed but stale' and instructs 'Run: bd setup claude'. bd actively claims ownership and considers the file out of date right now.
- 'bd setup codex --check' reports AGENTS.md, .codex/hooks.json and .agents/skills/beads/SKILL.md as installed and current.

CONSEQUENCE: the CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md difference is not policy drift. It is bd template-version skew between two recipe installs (block hash 6cd5cc61 stale vs 970c3bf2 current). Nobody ever decided the 'bd dolt push' line; a template did. Extracting these files into canonical/policy would have forked vendor boilerplate into our source of truth, where it would rot against future bd versions and be overwritten by the next bd setup.

WHAT THIS BEAD NOW DOES:
1. Record three ownership classes in SUBSTRATE.md terms:
   CANONICAL  - authored by us. Today: README.md, BASELINE.md. Policy content: currently NONE.
   VENDOR     - owned by another tool's installer; regenerated by it; verifiable via its own check command. Today: CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md, .claude/settings.json, .codex/*, .agents/skills/beads/*.
   PROJECTED  - derived by bin/ms from canonical.
2. EXPERIMENT, in a throwaway copy of this repo, never the live tree: add sentinel content to CLAUDE.md both INSIDE and OUTSIDE the BEGIN/END BEADS INTEGRATION markers, run 'bd setup claude', and record precisely what bd preserves and what it replaces.
3. From that result, determine the composition seam: whether our policy can coexist in a vendor file (out-of-marker region survives) or must live in a separate file the harness composes.

Do not run 'bd setup claude' in the live repo. Do not write canonical policy fragments in this bead.
design:
OWNERSHIP TABLE — every path present in the repo, one class each (verified 2026-08-31 via git ls-files, git log, and bd setup --check).

CANONICAL (authored by us; the substrate's source of truth)
  README.md                        commit 479ee18 'Initialize machine-state'
  BASELINE.md                      commit 4e74e46, hand-written inventory
  Policy content: NONE EXISTS YET. No human has authored a line of agent policy in this repo.

VENDOR (owned by bd's installers; regenerated by them; verify with bd setup <recipe> --check)
  CLAUDE.md                        recipe: claude   marker-delimited block + template stubs
  AGENTS.md                        recipe: codex    TWO marker blocks (INTEGRATION + CODEX SETUP)
  .claude/settings.json            recipe: claude   SessionStart hook, whole-file JSON
  .codex/config.toml               recipe: codex
  .codex/hooks.json                recipe: codex
  .agents/skills/beads/**          recipe: codex    bd owns the beads/ subdir, NOT the skills/ parent
  .beads/**                        bd's own data dir, incl. tracked config.yaml, metadata.json,
                                   hooks/*, README.md, .gitignore, and generated issues.jsonl
  .gitignore                       written by bd init; SPECIAL CASE, see below

PROJECTED (derived by bin/ms from canonical)
  Nothing yet.

SPECIAL CASE — .gitignore: vendor-authored but carries NO marker pair, only a comment header
('# Beads / Dolt files (added by bd init)'). It is co-owned by convention rather than protocol.
bd writes it at init, not on every setup, so the practical risk is low, but the substrate must
append its own commented section and must never rewrite the file whole.

SPECIAL CASE — .beads/issues.jsonl: untracked, NOT gitignored, and regenerated automatically
(export.auto: true in config.yaml). Vendor-generated data that will keep reappearing in
git status. Classify VENDOR-GENERATED; the substrate must not manage it.

COMPOSITION SEAM — chosen, justified by the machine-state-9tw.2 experiment

  Claude   splice ./CLAUDE.md   marker 'MACHINE-STATE POLICY'
  Codex    splice ./AGENTS.md   marker 'MACHINE-STATE POLICY'

Both files are VENDOR-owned but splice-safe: the experiment proved bd replaces only its own
marker pair, leaves foreign blocks in the same file untouched, appends at EOF when its markers
are absent, and removes only its own block. Using the same marker name for both agents means
both harnesses receive identical canonical policy through an identical mechanism — which is
precisely the interchangeability the epic is trying to buy.

Rejected alternative: an @import line in the vendor file pointing at a wholly-projected
POLICY.md. The sentinel proved such a line survives every bd operation, but it depends on
harness import support that is unverified for Codex, and it leaves one unmanaged line in a file
we do not own. Splice needs no such support.

GOVERNING PRINCIPLE (generalised from the experiment)
  Own the smallest addressable region, never the container.
    - within a file: our marker pair, never the whole file
    - within a directory: our own subdirectory, never the shared parent
bd follows exactly this rule (it owns .agents/skills/beads/, not .agents/skills/), which is why
co-tenancy works at all. The substrate adopts it as law.

CONSEQUENCE for machine-state-9tw.4: the planned 'link ~/.claude/skills' target is WRONG — it
claims a container another installer may later populate. Link individual skill directories
(~/.claude/skills/<name>) instead. Note also that ~/.agents/skills/ is a potential vendor path,
since bd's codex recipe has a --global variant that installs ~/.agents/skills/beads/; sibling
skill subdirectories there remain safe.
acceptance_criteria:
- Ownership classes recorded, with every current repo path assigned to exactly one class.
- DONE: experiment run in throwaway copies; behaviour recorded verbatim in notes.
- DONE: live repo verified byte-identical to 4d81b55 after the experiment.
- Composition seam chosen for Claude and Codex and recorded in SUBSTRATE.md terms (recommendation: marker-delimited splice; see machine-state-9tw.3).
notes:
SUPERSEDED PROPOSAL (2026-08-31): an earlier plan in this bead proposed extracting these files into canonical/policy fragments (00-generated, 10-identity, 20-task-tracking, 30-authority, 40-session-close, 50-shell-hygiene, agents/*). Withdrawn — it treated vendor boilerplate as our policy. The disposition table it produced remains useful only as evidence that 100% of both files is bd-generated.

NOTED SEPARATELY: CLAUDE.md is stale per 'bd setup claude --check'. Refreshing it is a vendor-maintenance action, not substrate work. Do not fold it into this bead.

EXPERIMENT RESULT (2026-08-31, bd 1.2.2, throwaway copies under scratchpad/exp1 and exp2; live repo verified byte-identical to 4d81b55 before and after).

METHOD: planted sentinels inside and outside the managed markers, ran the real recipes, diffed.

CLAUDE.md / 'bd setup claude' — output: 'Updated existing beads section in CLAUDE.md'. Diff was exactly 3 lines, ALL inside the markers:
  - hash 6cd5cc61 -> 970c3bf2
  - in-block sentinel deleted
  - 'bd dolt push' line added
  SURVIVED: modified H1, line immediately above BEGIN, an @import-style line, line below END.
  REMOVED: only the in-block sentinel.
  This confirms the template-skew theory outright: after setup, CLAUDE.md is byte-equal to the AGENTS.md block. The 'bd dolt push' difference was never a decision.

AGENTS.md / 'bd setup codex' — diff was ONE line: the sentinel inside the CODEX SETUP block. The sentinel inside the BEADS INTEGRATION block in the same file SURVIVED, because that block belongs to a different recipe. Block ownership is PER-RECIPE, not per-file.

--remove: surgical. Removed only its own block and its SessionStart hook; every out-of-marker sentinel survived. Leaves .claude/settings.json as {"hooks":{}} rather than deleting it.

Re-install onto a MARKERLESS file: 'Added beads section to existing CLAUDE.md' — appended at the end, all pre-existing content preserved. bd never claims the whole file.

CONCLUSION: bd is a well-behaved co-tenant. It owns a marker-delimited region, appends if absent, replaces in place if present, removes cleanly, and ignores other owners' markers.

THEREFORE co-ownership of CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md is SAFE, but only if our projector also confines itself to a region. A whole-file render would delete bd's block, bd would re-append it on next setup, and ms diff would flag it forever — a ping-pong loop.

INCIDENTAL BD BUG: 'bd setup <recipe> --check' ignores the global -C flag and inspects the real cwd (reports '✗ No hooks installed' for a correctly-installed copy). Any tooling that shells out to it must cd, not use -C.
close_reason: Ownership table complete (every repo path classified), bd rewrite behaviour verified experimentally, composition seam chosen: splice into CLAUDE.md and AGENTS.md with marker 'MACHINE-STATE POLICY'. Live repo byte-identical to 4d81b55 throughout.

title: Authenticate Proton Drive and demonstrate one real operation
description:
The CLI has been installed and verified since 2026-09-06 and has never been authenticated: 'proton-drive filesystem list /' prints 'You need to login first' and exits 1, promptly and without prompting. Everything the record claims about the tool is therefore claimed about a tool that has never talked to the account.

The blocker is gone. canonical/tooling/proton-drive.md says the CLI has nowhere to put a session because org.freedesktop.secrets is not activatable; that was true on 2026-09-05 and is not true now — gnome-keyring answers, and PROTON_DRIVE_CREDENTIALS_STORE is deliberately unset, so the session goes to the Secret Service under service ch.proton.drive/drive-sdk-cli.

AUTHENTICATION IS THE USER'S STEP and the record says so: 'auth login' opens a browser, and no agent should try to complete it.
design:
1. The user runs 'proton-drive auth login' and completes it in the browser. A keyring unlock prompt is expected during the write, because the login collection is currently LOCKED; the password it wants is the login password.

2. Confirm where the session actually landed rather than assuming: the login collection gains an item, and its attributes name service ch.proton.drive/drive-sdk-cli. If it landed in Default_keyring instead, that changes machine-state-t0u.11's migration plan.

3. Demonstrate one real operation — 'filesystem list /' — which is also the first proof that the recorded tool does the thing the record says it does.

4. THE FAILURE PATH, and it is the interesting one. Lock the login collection again (Service.Lock over D-Bus) and re-run 'filesystem list /'. Two possible behaviours and they are very different to live with: it PROMPTS for the unlock, or it reports 'You need to login first' and exits 1 — silently unauthenticated because the store is locked rather than because the session is gone. Whichever it does goes in the record, because on this machine the login keyring is locked more often than not (machine-state-t0u.11).
acceptance_criteria: 'proton-drive filesystem list /' returns real Drive content. The item is shown to live in a named keyring with named attributes. The locked-store behaviour is demonstrated, not guessed, and canonical/tooling/proton-drive.md is updated to replace its 'cannot be authenticated' paragraph with what actually happened.
notes:
DONE 2026-09-06 14:17, all four design steps, and the failure path came out the good way.

The user completed 'proton-drive auth login' in the browser and answered the keyring prompt. The item, read back off the bus:

  collection  login  (NOT Default_keyring — the default alias resolves to login now)
  label       ch.proton.drive/drive-sdk-cli/auth-session
  attributes  service=ch.proton.drive/drive-sdk-cli, account=auth-session,
              xdg:schema=com.oven-sh.bun.Secret

That schema is the surprise worth keeping: the credential goes through BUN'S secrets API, not libsecret directly — the same embedded runtime that makes the binary 112 MiB. Storage behaviour therefore belongs to Bun, and a Bun change can move it without Proton changing anything.

'proton-drive filesystem list /' returns the real top level (/my-files, /devices, /shared-by-me, /shared-with-me, /trash, /albums, /photos, /photos-shared-by-me, /photos-shared-with-me, /photos-trash), exit 0. Before the login the same command printed 'You need to login first' and exited 1.

THE LOCKED-STORE TEST, which was the point of step 4. The login collection was locked again over D-Bus (Secret.Service.Lock) and the command re-run. It raised a visible 'Unlock Login Keyring' prompt and WAITED. It did NOT fall back to 'You need to login first' — which would have made a locked keyring indistinguishable from a lost session, the failure mode this task was worried about. The user answered and the listing completed, exit 0.

The price of that correctness is a command that blocks until someone answers, on a machine where the login keyring is not reliably unlocked at boot (t0u.11) and an unanswered prompt is not withdrawn when its client dies (jw9). Anything running proton-drive unattended needs a timeout, and must read a timeout as 'the store was locked' rather than as an error from Drive.

Recorded in canonical/tooling/proton-drive.md, replacing its 'cannot be authenticated' paragraph.

LEFT FOR t0u.11: login holds exactly one item, the Drive session. Noctalia has NOT re-stored its master key there, and its old key sits in Default_keyring, which is locked.
close_reason: Authenticated, listing demonstrated, locked-store behaviour proven to prompt

title: A Secret Service write hangs until the collection object has been addressed once
description:
FOUND 2026-09-06 while verifying the PAM keyring change (machine-state-t0u.11), by trying to write a probe secret after the reboot.

Any Secret Service call that needs a prompt reaches /usr/lib/gcr-prompter, which logs that it created a GcrPromptDialog and began its secret exchange — and NO WINDOW EVER APPEARS. 'hyprctl clients' during the hang lists only the terminal. The caller then waits forever: 'secret-tool store' had to be killed the first time and exited 124 under 'timeout 10' the second. Read-only lookups ('secret-tool search') return instantly, so only operations that prompt are affected.

WHY IT MATTERS BEYOND THE KEYRING. Any tool that may ask for a secret — proton-drive, a browser, anything using libsecret — can hang with no visible cause and nothing on screen to answer. Until this is fixed, anything that might prompt must be run under 'timeout'.

WHAT IS NOT YET KNOWN: whether the dialog fails to map because gcr-prompter needs a portal or session component this desktop does not run, or because Hyprland is not showing it. gcr-prompter logs no error of its own — the only lines it writes are its normal 'Gcr:' trace.
acceptance_criteria: A prompt raised by a Secret Service write appears as a real window that can be answered, demonstrated by a 'secret-tool store' that completes; or, if prompting is deliberately not wired up here, the substrate records that and every secret path is designed not to prompt.
notes:
THE PREMISE IS FALSE, 2026-09-06 12:36-12:41, and the correction is worth more than the original claim.

PROMPTS RENDER FINE ON THIS COMPOSITOR. Driving the Secret Service directly from a small dbus-python probe — Service.Unlock on a collection path, then Prompt.Prompt("") on the returned prompt, on ONE connection so the prompt is not invalidated (scratchpad prompt_probe.py) — puts a real window on screen inside a second:

  hyprctl clients -> class "gcr-prompter", title "Unlock Keyring"        (Default_keyring)
  hyprctl clients -> class "gcr-prompter", title "Unlock Login Keyring"  (login)

Dismissing leaves no residue. The earlier conclusion came from watching hyprctl during a hang that never got as far as showing anything, and reading absence as invisibility.

WHAT ACTUALLY HANGS. The login collection object is not registered on D-Bus until something addresses that exact path. In that state the daemon half-knows it: Service.Collections LISTS /org/freedesktop/secrets/collection/login and ReadAlias("default") RESOLVES to it, while busctl tree omits it and a property Get returns "Object does not exist at path".

A write into the default collection while it is in that state makes the daemon begin prompting and then stop. gcr-prompter logs BeginPrompting, creates the GcrPromptDialog, begins the secret exchange, calls PromptReady — and the daemon NEVER calls PerformPrompt, which is the call that would display it. The client waits forever with nothing on screen. PerformPrompt arrives only when the client is killed, and is cancelled on arrival.

ONE Unlock REQUEST AGAINST THE PATH MATERIALISES THE OBJECT. Afterwards busctl tree lists it, property reads answer (Locked=true, Label "Login", 0 items), and 'secret-tool store' raises a NORMAL, VISIBLE password prompt instead of hanging. Same command, same session, same daemon — the object's existence is the entire difference.

THE OPERATIONAL RULE SURVIVES THE CORRECTION, for a different reason: anything that may touch the Secret Service still needs a timeout, because the hang is real for any collection that has not been addressed once since the daemon started.

A SECOND FACT, learned by leaving one: killing the client does NOT withdraw its prompt. The "Unlock Login Keyring" window stayed on screen after secret-tool was killed and only went away when gcr-prompter itself was killed. Anything that raises a prompt on this machine must clean up after itself.

AND A NEW PROBLEM FOR t0u.11. The login keyring reports Locked=true now, hours after gkr-pam logged "unlocked login keyring" at 10:48:01. Whether it was ever unlocked on the bus this boot cannot be recovered after the fact — the object did not exist to be asked. The test is a single query, first thing after the next boot, before anything else touches a secret.

title: The keyring that exists is not the one PAM unlocks, and noctalia already put a key in it
description:
FOUND 2026-09-06 while preparing the PAM auto-unlock change, by checking the machine before applying it.

Installing gnome-keyring had an immediate second-order effect that nothing predicted: NOCTALIA WROTE ITS MASTER STORAGE KEY INTO THE KEYRING as soon as a Secret Service appeared. Item label 'Noctalia encrypted storage key', attributes application=noctalia, name=master-key, owner=encrypted-state, scope=storage, xdg:schema=dev.noctalia.Secret. ~/.local/state/noctalia/state.toml has carried security_migrations.calendar_credentials_v1 = true since 2026-08-30, so noctalia has been waiting for a Secret Service for a week.

THE PROBLEM. The keyring holding it was AUTO-CREATED at 09:09:45 with no prompt and no interaction, is named 'Default_keyring' (~/.local/share/keyrings/Default_keyring.keyring, with ~/.local/share/keyrings/default pointing at it), and reports Locked=false. There is NO 'login' keyring.

That matters because pam_gnome_keyring unlocks the keyring named 'login', using the login password. It does not touch a keyring named Default_keyring. So applying the PAM change ALONE would produce a login keyring that nothing uses, while the default keyring — the one that actually receives secrets, including the future proton-drive session — stays outside the login password's protection.

Whatever protects Default_keyring, it is not the login password, because no password was ever supplied to create it. Created non-interactively with none available, which points at an empty passphrase; NOT independently confirmed, because confirming it means locking noctalia's key store and attempting an unlock, and that risks disrupting a live desktop component for a fact that does not change the fix.

WHAT THE FIX HAS TO ACHIEVE: a 'login' keyring created and unlocked by PAM from the login password, made the default, with noctalia's key and the proton-drive session living in it — and Default_keyring gone once nothing needs it.

ORDERING, and why the obvious order is wrong. Deleting Default_keyring first would take noctalia's master key with it. Its key was minted today and there is no encrypted payload on disk yet, so regeneration is very likely harmless — but 'very likely' is not a basis for deleting a key from a live desktop. Verify PAM works FIRST, then migrate, then delete.
design:
Three steps, each verifiable before the next, and only the first needs root.

1. Apply /etc/pam.d/greetd (two optional lines; the exact file is prepared and diffed, see machine-state-t0u.10.md section 3). Log out and back in.
2. Confirm login.keyring exists and reports Locked=false without a prompt having appeared. That is the whole test of the PAM change and it is independent of everything below.
3. Point ~/.local/share/keyrings/default at login, let noctalia re-store its key there, and remove Default_keyring only after confirming nothing still reads it.

Both PAM lines are 'optional', so neither can block a login. The auth line must sit AFTER 'auth include system-local-login' or no password is available to capture. Install the package before editing PAM — already satisfied, /usr/lib/security/pam_gnome_keyring.so is present.

The vendor conflict stands and is recorded in canonical/tooling/gnome-keyring.md: /etc/pam.d/greetd is owned by the greetd package AND was already edited once by noctalia (backup greetd.bak.noctalia.20260830145901 beside it). A future noctalia run can revert our two lines, and that failure is quiet — login keeps working and the keyring silently starts prompting again. If auto-unlock ever stops working, look there first.
acceptance_criteria: login.keyring exists, is the default, and is unlocked at login with no prompt. Noctalia's master key and the proton-drive session both live in it. Default_keyring is gone, and nothing broke when it went. The claim that PAM auto-unlock works is demonstrated by a locked-state query after a real login, not inferred from the file having been edited.
notes:
PAM CHANGE IS APPLIED, 2026-09-06 10:38 — /etc/pam.d/greetd is 360 bytes and carries both optional lines. Backup at /etc/pam.d/greetd.bak.machine-state.20260906, verified byte-identical to the pre-change file, so rollback is a cp in the other direction.

FIRST ATTEMPT FAILED SILENTLY AND WAS NOT A REVERT. After the first apply the file still had its original 2026-08-30 mtime: the sudo cp backup ran, the install never did. Not noctalia and not dcg — 'dcg explain' returns ALLOW for that exact command. Most likely the long scratchpad path was mangled on paste. Worth remembering: an unchanged mtime distinguishes 'never written' from 'written then reverted', and those have completely different causes.

STILL NO login.keyring AFTER TWO LOGOUT/LOGIN CYCLES, and the cause is now established rather than guessed:

  gnome-keyring-daemon has been running since 09:07:18 — before the PAM change and across both re-logins.
  Its cgroup is user.slice/user-1000.slice/user@1000.service/app.slice/dbus-...org.freedesktop.secrets@0.service
  logind KillUserProcesses = false (the Arch default, confirmed on the bus, not just in the commented conf)

So the D-Bus-activated daemon lives in the systemd USER MANAGER, which is not torn down at logout. pam_gnome_keyring's session phase with auto_start finds a daemon already owning the name and does nothing, every time. A LOGOUT CAN NEVER TEST THIS CHANGE ON THIS MACHINE. Only a reboot, or loginctl terminate-user, produces a login where no keyring daemon is already running.

That is a general trap for anything wired into PAM here, not a fact about gnome-keyring: with KillUserProcesses=no, a session-scoped mechanism tested by logging out is being tested against the previous session's processes.

SECOND SHADOWING PROBLEM, still unaddressed. ~/.local/share/keyrings/default points at Default_keyring, so even once login.keyring exists, new secrets go to the old keyring. Removing that 15-byte pointer would let gnome-keyring fall back to login as the default. It was NOT removed: the Claude Code permission classifier blocked the rm, and that is left for the user rather than worked around. Both files are backed up and verified byte-identical under the session scratchpad (keyring-backup/), and Default_keyring.keyring itself was never touched, so noctalia's key is intact on disk.

NEXT: reboot, then check whether login.keyring exists and reports Locked=false with no prompt having appeared. That single query is the whole test of the PAM change.

THE REBOOT SETTLED IT, 2026-09-06 10:47:15 boot. The PAM change WORKS, and only a reboot could show it, exactly as the previous session predicted. greetd's journal for this boot:

  10:48:01 greetd[1113]: pam_unix(greetd:session): session opened for user klaas
  10:48:01 greetd[1113]: gkr-pam: unlocked login keyring

~/.local/share/keyrings/login.keyring was created at 10:48, 105 bytes, internal name "Login" — a fresh empty keyring. No prompt appeared. Step 2 of the design passes.

(The 10:47:27 line "gkr-pam: couldn't unlock the login keyring" is the GREETER's own session, uid 962, and is unrelated. Read the uid before reading the message.)

THE SHADOWING POINTER IS GONE. ~/.local/share/keyrings/default no longer exists, and ReadAlias("default") on the Secret Service now returns /org/freedesktop/secrets/collection/login. New secrets are aimed at the login keyring.

BUT THE LOGIN COLLECTION IS NOT REACHABLE ON D-BUS, and this is the new blocker. The daemon lists it (Service.Collections includes .../collection/login) and resolves the default alias to it, yet:

  busctl get-property .../collection/login ... Locked -> "Object does not exist at path"
  busctl tree org.freedesktop.secrets       -> shows Default_5fkeyring and session, NOT login

CONSEQUENCE, demonstrated twice. 'secret-tool store' into the default collection hangs forever. It reaches gcr-prompter, which logs "creating new GcrPromptDialog" and begins a secret exchange — and NO WINDOW EVER APPEARS. hyprctl clients during the hang lists only the terminal. So the prompt cannot be answered, and the caller waits indefinitely. First attempt had to be killed; second was run under 'timeout 10' and exited 124. A read-only 'secret-tool search' returns instantly, so only writes are affected.

That is a workstation-level fact, not a keyring one: a gcr prompt on this compositor is an invisible, unanswerable hang. Anything that may prompt for a secret must be run with a timeout until that is fixed.

DEFAULT_KEYRING IS NOW LOCKED (Locked=true after the reboot), still holding noctalia's master key as item 1. Nothing has unlocked it this boot, which answers the open question the other way from the guess: it is not passphrase-free-and-auto-unlocked in a fresh session. Noctalia has not re-stored its key into login either.

NEXT, and step 3 is blocked until the prompt problem has an answer: migrating noctalia's key and deleting Default_keyring both need a write path into the login collection, and every write currently ends in an invisible prompt.

THE STEP-2 CLAIM NEEDS A QUALIFIER, 2026-09-06 12:41. Investigating machine-state-jw9 materialised the login collection on D-Bus, and it answers:

  Locked = true, Label = "Login", Items = 0

That is hours after gkr-pam logged "unlocked login keyring" at 10:48:01. So what is demonstrated is that PAM RAN AND REPORTED SUCCESS, and that the keyring file was created — NOT that the Secret Service sees an unlocked keyring. Those are different claims and this record should not blur them.

It cannot be settled retroactively: before jw9's Unlock the collection object did not exist to be asked, so there is no way to know whether it was ever unlocked on the bus this boot, or was unlocked and later locked.

THE TEST IS ONE QUERY, FIRST THING AFTER THE NEXT BOOT, before anything else touches a secret:

  busctl --user get-property org.freedesktop.secrets \
    /org/freedesktop/secrets/collection/login \
    org.freedesktop.Secret.Collection Locked

false -> PAM's unlock reaches the Secret Service, and today's true was caused by something later in the session.
true  -> the PAM unlock does not reach the bus at all, and auto-unlock needs a different mechanism than the one this task assumed.

title: Establish a quieter ASUS gaming profile
description: Use the ASUS control stack to understand and reduce unnecessary fan noise during moderate gaming loads on the ROG Strix SCAR 18 G835LXG, without compromising safe thermal limits. The motivating observation from Dyson Sphere Program was approximately 40-48% GPU utilization, 79-87 W GPU power, 46-48 C GPU temperature, 48-49 C CPU package temperature, and fans around 2700/3000/3400 RPM. The machine was cool; the issue is acoustic policy rather than overheating.
design: Share installation and hardware discovery with machine-state-t0u.8's asusctl/asusd work, but keep thermal/performance control distinct from RGB. First inventory firmware performance profiles and read-only sensor/fan/TDP capabilities. Prefer a vendor-defined quieter profile over custom curves. If custom curves are later justified, preserve firmware failsafes, never lower thermal ceilings, change one dimension at a time, and retain an immediate route back to the stock profile. Treat fan curves, CPU/GPU power limits, boost behavior, MUX/GPU modes, and charge limits as separate controls rather than a single Armoury-style switch.
acceptance_criteria: Install nothing except through the explicitly approved shared asusctl step. Record idle and representative-game baselines for CPU/GPU temperature, power, utilization, and all three fan speeds. Enumerate available stock profiles and test the least invasive quieter profile during the same workload. Confirm temperatures stabilize safely, performance remains acceptable, sleep/resume and AC/battery transitions behave correctly, and reverting restores stock behavior. Do not begin with custom curves or alter TDP, GPU mode, MUX, charge limits, or firmware thermal protections.
notes:
INVENTORY DONE 2026-09-06, read-only, and it changes the plan: THE ACOUSTIC WORK NEEDS NO INSTALL AT ALL.

The kernel already carries this laptop. Loaded: asus_wmi, asus_nb_wmi, asus_armoury, hid_asus. Nothing from the asusctl stack is installed and nothing needs to be for profiles or fans.

WHAT IS ALREADY EXPOSED

  /sys/firmware/acpi/platform_profile        = balanced
  /sys/firmware/acpi/platform_profile_choices = quiet balanced performance

power-profiles-daemon is ACTIVE and powerprofilesctl is on PATH, mapping performance/balanced/power-saver onto the firmware profiles, all three on the intel_pstate + platform_profile drivers. So 'powerprofilesctl set power-saver' selects the firmware QUIET profile over D-Bus — no root, no install, instantly reversible. That is the least invasive quieter profile the design asked for, and it was here all along.

  hwmon 'asus'                    3 fans, labelled cpu_fan / gpu_fan / mid_fan
  hwmon 'asus_custom_fan_curve'   pwm1..pwm3, EIGHT auto points each (temp + pwm),
                                  pwm{1,2,3}_enable currently 2 (firmware curve)
  hwmon 'coretemp'                25 temperature inputs
  /sys/class/power_supply/BAT0/charge_control_end_threshold = 100

Custom fan curves are therefore a KERNEL interface, not an asusctl feature — asusctl would be a friendlier front-end to the same eight points, not the thing that unlocks them. That matters for the install decision in t0u.8: lighting is the only capability that actually requires the daemon.

IDLE BASELINE, balanced profile, 2026-09-06 14:57

  cpu_fan 1800 rpm   gpu_fan 1600 rpm   mid_fan 1900 rpm
  CPU package 36-38 C
  GPU 30 C, 23-27 W, 0-18 percent

Compare the motivating Dyson Sphere Program observation: 2700/3000/3400 rpm at 46-49 C. The machine spins up roughly 1000 rpm per fan for a load that moves temperature by about 10 C, which is the acoustic policy this task exists to question.

A SAMPLER EXISTS, read-only, in the session scratchpad: asus-sample.sh writes time, profile, three fan speeds, CPU package temperature and GPU temperature/power/utilisation to a CSV in ~/.cache every N seconds. Smoke-tested. It changes nothing; it only reads sysfs and nvidia-smi.

NEXT, and it needs the user because it needs the game: sample under Dyson Sphere Program on balanced, switch to power-saver mid-session with 'powerprofilesctl set power-saver', keep sampling, and compare the same workload on both profiles. Only if quiet is inadequate does a custom curve become the question, and the curve interface is already there when it does.

MEASURED UNDER THE ACTUAL GAME, 2026-09-06 15:55-16:05, Dyson Sphere Program, one uninterrupted sampling run at 2 s intervals across a live profile switch. Steady state only (the balanced ramp and the first 90 s after the switch discarded), load-matched to GPU utilisation >= 25 percent so both sides describe the same kind of work.

  balanced  n=90   fans 2694/2994/3333   cpu 46.2 C  gpu 42.4 C  63.7 W  util 36%
  quiet     n=51   fans 1800/1600/1898   cpu 52.0 C  gpu 48.5 C  65.0 W  util 43%

THE STOCK QUIET PROFILE IS THE ANSWER. Roughly a third off the CPU fan and nearly half off the GPU and mid fans — 894, 1394 and 1435 rpm — for 5.8 C on the CPU and 6.1 C on the GPU. Peak CPU was 55 C on quiet against 56 C on balanced. Nothing on this machine is thermally interesting at those numbers.

THE FANS ON QUIET SIT AT EXACTLY THEIR IDLE SPEEDS — 1800/1600/1900, the same figures measured at 38 C — while the machine runs at 52 C under load. The quiet curve has not begun to ramp at all yet, so the headroom is not being spent; it is being ignored, which is what a curve is supposed to do.

A WORRY THAT MEASUREMENT KILLED. Early samples suggested quiet capped GPU power (53.5 W against 64.6 W), which would have traded frames for silence. At steady state it draws slightly MORE — 65.0 W at 43 percent utilisation against 63.7 W at 36 percent. The early figure was a lower-load transient, not a cap. The user independently reported no perceptible degradation while playing.

SO NO CUSTOM CURVE IS NEEDED FOR THIS WORKLOAD, which is the outcome the design asked for: prefer a vendor-defined quieter profile over custom curves. The eight-point interface is there when a workload finally justifies it, and asusctl reads the curves per profile with --get-enabled, all currently 'enabled: false' with the firmware in control.

STILL OPEN, and they are the acceptance criteria this run did not touch: sleep/resume behaviour, AC/battery transitions, and a heavier or longer workload than DSP before quiet becomes the AC default. asusd currently holds AC=Balanced, Battery=Quiet, with quiet set as the ACTIVE profile only — so a reboot or a power-source change reverts it, deliberately.
close_reason: Quiet profile established, measured against balanced under the real game, and made the default on AC and battery; remaining transition tests split into their own issue

title: A package-based tooling record cannot report a tool absent, so the declaration SUBSTRATE.md §7.2 makes does not hold for three of them
description:
SUBSTRATE.md §7.2: 'a tooling record is the declaration that this machine should have the thing', and ms status fails when a recorded tool is absent rather than labelling it not installed and moving on. That is true only for records whose command is the tool's own binary.

ms status uses a record's 'missing' label only when the check command cannot be EXECUTED (rc is None from subprocess). pacman executes perfectly well while reporting that a package is not installed: 'pacman -Qkk steam' on an absent package prints "error: package 'steam' was not found" and exits 1. Exit 1 routes to 'fail'.

So for proton-mail, proton-pass and steam, an uninstalled package reads as 'files altered or missing' — a misleading label — is never added to the absent list, and does not fail the run. The three records that most look like a declaration of desired state are the three that cannot enforce one.

Found 2026-09-05 while writing canonical/tooling/steam.md before the install, which is exactly the state that exposes it: the record exists, the package does not, and ms status neither says so correctly nor fails.

canonical/tooling/proton-pass.md states the same observation — 'pacman -Qkk on an absent package exits 1' — and concludes 'so the missing path can fail'. The observation is right and the conclusion is wrong; exit 1 is the fail path, not the missing path. That sentence needs correcting wherever it appears.
design:
NOT a fix to guess at. An exit code cannot distinguish 'the subject does not exist' from 'the subject is broken' when the tool uses 1 for both, so ms cannot infer it. The shape that fits this repository is a record that DECLARES the difference rather than one ms infers: a separate presence probe whose failure means absent, distinct from the integrity check whose failure means broken. For a package that is 'pacman -Q <pkg>' against 'pacman -Qkk <pkg>'. For a binary the two collapse into one, which is why the gap was invisible until a package-based record was written.

Whatever is chosen must not weaken the existing binary case, and needs a negative control: a record for a package that is genuinely not installed must fail the run and say 'not installed', and disabling the mechanism must make that assertion fail.
acceptance_criteria: An uninstalled package with a tooling record reports 'not installed', is counted absent, and fails the run — the same meaning a missing binary already has. The binary case is unchanged and still proven. A negative control disables the new distinction and shows the assertion then misses the absent package. SUBSTRATE.md §7.2's claim is either made true for every record shape or narrowed to the shapes where it holds. The wrong conclusion in canonical/tooling/proton-pass.md is corrected.
notes:
FIXED 2026-09-05. A record now DECLARES the difference instead of ms inferring it: an optional 'presence' probe beside 'check'. The probe failing means absent; the check failing means broken. For a binary the two collapse into one command, which is why the gap was invisible until a package-based record existed.

bin/ms: a third state, not two. presence rc 0 -> present, run the check. rc non-zero -> absent: missing label, counted absent, run fails, check and wiring skipped. rc None (the probe itself could not run) -> UNOBSERVED, carried from the record, NOT counted absent — a missing pacman is not evidence that every package is uninstalled. read_tool_checks also admits a record carrying only 'presence'.

Records: presence = 'pacman -Q <pkg>' added to steam, proton-pass, proton-mail.

Proven against real pacman in a throwaway copy with HOME redirected, a record for a package that does not exist: with the presence line, 'not installed' + 'recorded here but not installed' + exit 1; with that one line deleted and nothing else changed, 'files altered or missing', not counted absent, run passes. That is the reported bug reproduced and closed.

tests/acceptance.py: 22 (absent package reports absent), 23 (an unobservable probe is carried, not counted, and does not pass the check off as seen), 22n (probe removed -> 22 misses it). 33/33. cap 44/44, machine 11/11. Binary case unchanged: 17, 17n, 18, 18n still pass.

Docs: SUBSTRATE.md 7.2 gains the paragraph making its claim true for every record shape; proton-pass.md's 'so the missing path can fail' corrected and pointed at the presence line; steam.md's open gap rewritten as closed, with the two-way demonstration; proton-mail.md gains the same note.
close_reason: Presence probe added; every acceptance criterion met and proven both ways against real pacman.

title: ms writes environment-dependent verdicts into state/tooling.json, so a lean session dirties the tree and can report false changes
description:
state/tooling.json is committed inventory, but every ms run overwrites it with whatever the current environment could observe. Reproduced 2026-09-05: 'env -i PATH=/usr/bin HOME=$HOME ms status' rewrote four fields — hypr version 0.56.2 -> '-' (hyprctl needs HYPRLAND_INSTANCE_SIGNATURE), dcg active -> degraded, claude guarded true -> false, claude version 2.1.259 -> 2.1.261.

This was found because the working tree was already dirty at session start with exactly this shape: hypr version '-' plus proton-mail and proton-pass flipped to 'files altered or missing'. Running ms status from a full shell restored the file to match HEAD. The SessionStart hook runs 'ms changes', so the hook itself is a source of the contamination.

Two consequences, the second worse than the first: the tree goes dirty for no reason a reader can attribute, and 'ms changes' compares against a mark that a degraded run may have written, so it can announce a change that never happened — or, having recorded a degraded verdict as the new truth, stay silent about a real one.
acceptance_criteria: A run that cannot obtain a verdict does not persist one — the previous recorded value survives, distinguishable from an observed value. Reproduce the stripped-environment run and show state/tooling.json unchanged. The distinction is falsifiable: a test that disables it must fail. Decide and record whether 'ms changes' may write a mark at all from a non-interactive hook.
notes:
CORRECTION to this record as filed. It said the SessionStart hook was a source of the tooling.json contamination. It is not: 'ms changes' writes state/machine.json only, never state/tooling.json. The contaminating command is 'ms status', which rewrote the inventory on every run. The hook had a smaller version of the same fault — without a mark it would take one, and --quiet is the hook form — and that is fixed too.

DIAGNOSIS. Two environment-dependent verdicts, both reproduced: 'hyprctl version' exits 1 without HYPRLAND_INSTANCE_SIGNATURE, so hypr's version was recorded as '-'; 'dcg doctor --strict' checks that dcg is on PATH, so a run without ~/.local/bin recorded dcg 'degraded' and claude 'guarded: false'. The tests are properly sandboxed (tmpdir copy, own HOME, PATH=/usr/bin:/bin) and were not the source.

NOT ATTRIBUTED, and recorded as unattributed rather than guessed: the 'files altered or missing' verdict on proton-mail and proton-pass seen at session start. pacman -Qkk exits 0 for both under every environment tried, and /var/log/pacman.log shows no activity since 2026-09-03 14:14, so it was not a real package change and not a mid-upgrade transient. Whatever produced it, the next ordinary run reverted it silently — which is the argument for the fix rather than against it.

DELIVERED. (1) A reading is OBSERVED or NOT OBSERVED and the two never look alike; what was not observed keeps what the record held and says so on its line. (2) A non-zero check resolved only via the remembered path is set aside — this run's PATH is not the machine's. (3) An unobserved guard is not reported UNGUARDED. (4) 'ms status' writes only on --record, matching 'ms changes'; differing readings are reported for a person to accept. (5) 'ms changes --quiet' will not take the first mark.

PROVEN FALSIFIABLE. Three negative controls: write gate removed -> a plain status run rewrites the inventory; carry-over removed -> a known version is recorded as '-'; hook guard removed -> the quiet run freezes the mark. 30/30 assertions.

SIDE EFFECT WORTH NOTING: 'ms status' is listed in the skill as a free read-only action. It now is one.
close_reason: ms status reports and only records on --record, matching ms changes; unobserved readings carry the recorded value and say so; a check reached only by remembered path no longer yields a machine verdict; ms changes --quiet will not take the first mark. Three negative controls, 30/30.

title: Notice what changed on the machine, by querying the package db rather than watching it
description:
WHAT THIS IS FOR. When software is installed, updated or removed on this machine, that should reach
the agent and the human durably, rather than being discovered by accident later. Beads are the
destination because they survive across sessions; a desktop notification does not.

THE DESIGN, and why it is a query rather than a watcher.

The first design was a systemd user path unit watching /var/log/pacman.log, reactive and needing no
privilege. It is the wrong shape. A watcher only sees events WHILE IT IS RUNNING — a reboot, a
crash, a week where nothing ran, and the event is gone with no way to recover it.

The local pacman database already records an install date per package. So "what changed since I last
looked" is a plain query against authoritative state:

    expac '%l\t%n %v' | sort -r

That is retroactive, cannot miss an event, needs no daemon, no systemd unit, no root, and no moving
parts. It also pairs correctly with beads: the high-water mark lives in recorded state rather than
in a process that has to stay alive.

RESOLUTION IS BY FILE OWNERSHIP, NOT BY NAME. `pacman -Qo $(command -v X)` is the correct question.
Matching a binary name against `pacman -Qq` is wrong and was wrong in practice: `codex` was
classified a loose binary needing root to update, when the file is owned by `openai-codex 0.151.0-1.1`
and updates like any other package. The package name and the binary name differ. This is the same
evidence-based technique already used by cap's vendor_owner().

THE LOOSE BINARIES HAVE NO DATABASE. After correcting the above, three remain: dcg, bd and claude,
all in ~/.local/bin, all user-writable, all carrying self-updaters. They need their own recorded
state — a content hash per binary — because nothing else records their version history.

SCOPE. Detect and report. Applying updates is NOT in scope here: repo packages need root, which is
the one real boundary on this machine, and a self-updater fetches a binary over the network, which
is a supply-chain step this repository has never taken. Both belong in their own decisions.
acceptance_criteria:
- `ms changes` reports packages installed, upgraded or removed since a recorded high-water mark, and
  content changes to the loose binaries that no package owns.
- It works retroactively: a change made while nothing was running is still reported.
- `ms changes --record` accepts the current state as seen.
- Provenance is resolved by `pacman -Qo` against the resolved binary path, never by name matching.
- Exit code distinguishes "changes pending" from "nothing changed", so it composes.
- A negative control proves the detection can fail: with the comparison disabled, a real change goes
  unreported.
close_reason: ms changes queries the package db rather than watching it: retroactive, no daemon, no root. Provenance by pacman -Qo on the resolved path. Two silent failures closed on the way — an unparsed expac format that recorded an empty inventory as success, and PATH-dependent resolution that would have dropped three tools and re-reported them as new. 20/20 acceptance with a negative control.

title: Decide whether desired installed state becomes a registry, or stays a human step
description:
BLOCKS machine-state-t0u. Decide once, before t0u.1, because the answer shapes all five children and
is expensive to change after two of them are done.

THE GAP, stated precisely. canonical/ holds roles, actions, bindings, desktop, hooks, policy, skills
and tooling. None of them declares that a piece of software SHOULD be present. A tooling record
describes a tool that IS installed and how to verify it; its `missing = "not installed"` label
reports absence and drives nothing.

So machine-state can answer "is Docker healthy?" and cannot answer "should this machine have
Docker?" — and therefore cannot answer "is this machine complete?" or "what would it take to rebuild
it?" t0u adds five pieces of software and makes that gap load-bearing for the first time.

THE OPTIONS, and what each actually costs:

  A. LEAVE IT. Installation stays an explicit human step; the tooling record is written afterwards
     and `ms status` verifies it from then on. Consistent with the operating rule that live-machine
     changes are separate and explicit, and with the existing seven records. Costs: no answer to
     "what should be here", and no rebuild path — the machine's contents remain discoverable only by
     looking at the machine.

  B. A PACKAGES/SERVICES REGISTRY under canonical/, declaring desired state; `ms status` reports
     drift between declared and installed, and REPORTS ONLY. Nothing installs. This is the smallest
     thing that answers the question, and it matches how every other registry here works: declare,
     derive, report, never act.

  C. B PLUS APPLY. A command that installs what is declared and missing. This crosses the boundary
     the whole substrate has kept so far — bin/ms writes files, bin/cap runs desktop actions, and
     neither installs software or touches systemd. It needs root, which is the one real boundary on
     this machine (CAPABILITIES.md section 6), and it would make canonical/ a thing that can install
     packages. That is a materially different security posture and should not be arrived at by
     drifting.

RECOMMENDATION: B. It answers the question that t0u exposes, keeps the declare/derive/report shape
every other registry has, and leaves the boundary where it is. A is defensible if the answer is that
this machine will never be rebuilt from its own description. C should be a separate, deliberate
decision if it is ever wanted, not a later increment of B.

RELATED, and worth deciding together because they are the same shape: systemd units. Docker and
Tailscale are services, and nothing here declares or verifies unit state either. If B happens, it
should cover services or explicitly say why not.

DO NOT start t0u.1 before this is answered.
acceptance_criteria:
- One of A, B or C is chosen and recorded in SUBSTRATE.md, with the reason and the rejected options.
- If B: the registry's shape is defined, and whether it covers systemd services as well as packages
  is answered explicitly rather than left to the first implementer.
- If A: SUBSTRATE.md states that this machine is not describable-to-rebuild, so the limit is a
  recorded choice rather than an omission.
- Whatever is chosen, t0u's five children are consistent with it before any of them starts.
close_reason: Decided: option B, implemented as a property of the tooling records rather than a new registry. Measurement settled it — the decision surface is 3 packages, not 1099 or 183, because 180 explicit packages arrived with the CachyOS install on 2026-08-30. A three-entry registry duplicating canonical/tooling/ would be BASELINE.md's mistake renamed. A tooling record now DECLARES the machine should have the thing, and ms status fails when a recorded tool is absent. Evidence was a live instance: proton-mail-bin had no record for two days while a role and a key binding depended on it. Deliberately does not install; declaring desired state and acting on it are different powers, and installation needs root. PATH sensitivity filed as machine-state-ayn.

title: Reading private keys and tokens is unguarded; secret_disclosure does not cover it
description:
Found while reviewing the dcg staged rollout (machine-state-3r1) on 2026-09-03.

secret_disclosure was enabled on 2026-08-31 with the recorded reason 'reading private keys and
tokens is unguarded today'. Eighteen dcg test probes show it still is. Every one of these is
ALLOWED with the pack enabled:

  reading an SSH private key from ~/.ssh
  printenv of an API-key environment variable
  reading ~/.aws/credentials
  gh auth token
  reading a .env file
  env | grep -i key
  literal sk-ant-... , ghp_... , sk-proj-... and AKIA... strings in a command
  a literal BEGIN OPENSSH PRIVATE KEY string

So the pack is enabled and, for every shape probed, inert. It is kept at 'warn' rather than
promoted, because promoting a pack that never matches would change nothing observable while making
it read as enforcement.

WHY THIS MATTERS HERE SPECIFICALLY. This machine's premise is that agents operate it. An agent that
can read a private key or an API token and put it in a command has crossed the boundary that
matters most, and nothing currently notices. dcg is designated the safety boundary beneath all
harnesses; this is the largest hole in it that has been measured.

WHAT TO ESTABLISH, in order:
  - what secret_disclosure's rules actually match. dcg exposes no rule listing ('dcg packs
    --expand' shows the pack tree only, '-vv' adds nothing), so this needs upstream docs or source.
  - whether another pack covers it (secrets.* are all disabled and are CLI-tool-specific:
    vault, doppler, infisical, onepassword, aws_secrets).
  - whether a project-level .dcg.toml can add patterns. That layer is enforcement-only, so it
    would be safe to manage from canonical/ — see canonical/tooling/dcg.md Layer.

DO NOT close this by promoting secret_disclosure to deny. That would look like a fix and change
nothing.
acceptance_criteria:
- What secret_disclosure actually matches is established from evidence, not inferred.
- Either the gap is closed by a rule that demonstrably blocks a private-key or token read, or the
  gap is recorded as unclosable with the reason.
- Any new rule is proven by a negative control: it must be shown to fail when disabled.
notes:
RESOLVED 2026-09-03. The pack was not broken; it was wrongly chosen.

WHAT secret_disclosure ACTUALLY MATCHES, from 'dcg pack info secret_disclosure' rather than from
inference: 11 destructive patterns, every one targeting a secret-manager CLI — infisical, op,
doppler, vault, and the AWS secrets and parameter-store subcommands. Its own description says so.
None of those five tools is installed on this machine, so the pack has no surface here. The 18
probes passed because it was never going to match them.

So it was enabled against the principle recorded in the same config — that rules for absent software
protect nothing. Kept enabled at warn anyway: it costs nothing measurable and is correct if one of
those CLIs is ever installed. What changed is that the record now says what it covers.

THE REAL GAP IS CLOSED by a custom pack, machinestate.secrets, at
~/.config/dcg/packs/local-secrets.yaml, loaded through custom_paths. Four rules: SSH private key
reads, credential-file reads (aws credentials, netrc, gh hosts, docker config, .env), printenv of a
credential-shaped variable, and the CLI subcommands that exist to print a live token.

VERIFIED: 26/26 on a probe suite of 12 dangerous and 14 legitimate commands — zero false positives,
including public-key reads, known_hosts, ssh config, grepping source for the word token, printenv
HOME and PATH, and reading .envrc. Proven by negative control: pointing custom_paths at an empty
directory leaves all four unguarded, and restoring it blocks all four.

KNOWN LIMIT, recorded rather than papered over: echo and printf are matched by NOTHING in dcg
0.13.9 — tested with an absolute /usr/bin path, with a literal word instead of a variable, and piped
onward. Variable references are not the obstacle; a reader with $HOME in the path blocks correctly.
So disclosure via echo cannot be guarded, and the rule names printenv only rather than listing echo
and failing silently.

THREE UNDOCUMENTED CUSTOM-PACK BEHAVIOURS, each cost time:
  - a pack with no 'keywords' matches nothing. dcg pack validate reports their absence as a
    performance suggestion; it is load-bearing. Keywords must be the executables, which are always
    present and lower case, not the secret-shaped words, which are neither.
  - the [packs] enabled list does NOT gate a custom pack. custom_paths alone activates it, which is
    why the negative control targets the load path.
  - 'dcg packs --enabled' lists a custom pack that 'dcg pack info' reports as not found.

All recorded in canonical/tooling/dcg.md.
close_reason: Established from dcg pack info that secret_disclosure covers secret-manager CLIs only, none of which are installed — correctly built, wrongly chosen. Gap closed by a custom pack machinestate.secrets: 26/26 probes, zero false positives, proven by negative control on the load path. Known limit recorded: echo and printf cannot be guarded in dcg 0.13.9.

title: MOD_ORDER advertises CTRL, which this compositor does not accept
description:
From the independent review (machine-state-8cy), finding 7 — but the finding's premise is wrong and
the real defect is larger.

The review asks whether Hyprland treats CTRL and CONTROL as aliases, and if so to normalize them.
EVIDENCE SAYS IT TREATS NEITHER: Hyprland 0.56.2's modifier name table is SHIFT, CONTROL, SUPER,
MOD4, META, MOD5, located adjacent to the hl.bind / hl.define_submap / 'unbind: bad argument'
strings, so it is the table the Lua binding path uses. CTRL does not appear. Live modmasks
corroborate the table: 68 = SUPER+CONTROL, 69 = SUPER+CONTROL+SHIFT, 72 = SUPER+ALT.

(hyprctl keyword cannot probe this: it answers 'keyword can't work with non-legacy parsers' under
the Lua config, so no runtime bind was created.)

So the bug is not a missed collision. MOD_ORDER contains CTRL, which ADVERTISES a spelling the
compositor rejects. A binding declared with CTRL renders hl.bind("CTRL + X", ...), fails to parse
at load, and cap preview reports it owned / ok — a key that does not exist, described as working.
That is the defect class this slice exists to prevent, reached from the opposite direction.

The fix is REJECTION at load, the way an unknown consequence class is rejected, not aliasing.
Aliasing would silently accept a declaration whose author was wrong about the target.

Modifier names are compositor facts, so the valid set belongs next to the thing that knows the
compositor, and the source of the list must be recorded.
acceptance_criteria:
- Declaring an unknown modifier name is rejected at load with a message naming the valid set.
- The valid set matches the compositor's own table, and where that list came from is recorded.
- A test asserts a CTRL declaration is refused, with a negative control.
close_reason: Fixed and tested; see commit. 8cy.2 uncovered that the focus dispatch used a call form invalid under the Lua config, so it had never worked while reporting ok.

title: Decide the ownership class of generated content under canonical/
description:
From the independent review (machine-state-8cy), finding 1. VERIFIED — this is a real contradiction
in the contract, not a style question.

SUBSTRATE.md section 1: 'Canonical content is what a human authored here.'
canonical/desktop/hypr/bindings.lua: 'Generated by bin/cap from canonical/bindings/. Do not edit by hand.'
adapters/hypr.toml then lists that generated file as a SOURCE for ms render.

So ms currently treats a derived intermediate as canonical input, and the document says canonical
means authored. One of the two has to change.

The options, and what each costs:
  - permit generated intermediates under canonical/ and say so explicitly, naming how they are
    distinguished from authored content;
  - move them to a derived location (state/ or a build/ directory) and let adapters name sources
    outside canonical/, which widens ms's source rules;
  - treat cap render's output as an adapter of its own rather than a source for another adapter.

DECIDE THIS BEFORE bru.7.5. The coordinator that phase evaluates needs a staging location, and
where staging may legitimately live is exactly this question.
acceptance_criteria:
- The ownership class of cap-generated output is stated in SUBSTRATE.md.
- Either the location changes or the contract does; the contradiction does not survive.
