- ms source-boundary rules are not weakened silently — any widening is explicit and reasoned.
- The decision names where bru.7.5's staging output may live.
close_reason: DERIVED added as a fourth ownership class; file moved to derived/hypr/bindings.lua; ms now enforces source eligibility at manifest load. Byte-transparent — ms project reports unchanged. Unblocks bru.7.5, whose staging location is answered: derived/.

title: render must apply the UNKNOWN-chord safeguard that check applies
description:
From the independent review of the capability slice (machine-state-8cy), finding 4. VERIFIED against bin/cap.

cmd_render filters only definite conflicts:

    conflicts = [c for c in (chord_of(b) for b in key_bindings()) if not check_chord(c)[0]]

unreadable_risk() is not called anywhere in cmd_render. So a chord whose modifier family matches a
vendor binding with a computed key — the UNKNOWN state introduced in bru.7.4 — renders cleanly, and
cap render then prints 'run ms project'. Only a later cap check reports it.

Rendering and checking must agree about what is safe to project. They are the same question asked at
two moments, and a gate that is laxer than the report it precedes is not a gate.

DECIDE, and record: does an UNKNOWN chord refuse the render outright, or render with a visible
warning? Refusing is consistent with how dangling references are treated. Warning is consistent with
UNKNOWN meaning 'not proven conflicted'. Pick one deliberately; do not leave render silent.
acceptance_criteria:
- cmd_render consults unreadable_risk for every declared chord.
- The refuse-versus-warn choice is made deliberately and recorded in the code.
- A test asserts render and check agree on an UNKNOWN chord, with a negative control.
close_reason: Fixed and tested; see commit. 8cy.2 uncovered that the focus dispatch used a call form invalid under the Lua config, so it had never worked while reporting ok.

title: Provider outcomes must derive from the command result, not be assumed
description:
From the independent review (machine-state-8cy), finding 5. VERIFIED against bin/cap.

do_ensure has two calls to hyprctl dispatch focuswindow. Both use capture_output=True and DISCARD
the return code, then 'return plan, "ok"'. A refused or failed dispatch is journalled as
outcome=ok.

state/actions.jsonl is the corpus this machine's provenance model rests on. Everywhere else in this
repository a surface that cannot support a claim says so; the action journal is currently the one
surface permitted to assert success it did not verify.

Minimum: outcome follows the dispatch return code. Better: verify post-state — after a focus, the
focused window is the one that was asked for — because a zero exit from hyprctl means the command
was accepted, not that the window took focus.
acceptance_criteria:
- Every provider returns an outcome derived from the command result.
- A failing dispatch produces a non-ok outcome in state/actions.jsonl.
- Where post-state can be verified cheaply, it is, and the distinction between 'accepted' and
  'verified' is explicit rather than implied.
- A test drives a failing dispatch and asserts the journal records the failure.
close_reason: Fixed and tested; see commit. 8cy.2 uncovered that the focus dispatch used a call form invalid under the Lua config, so it had never worked while reporting ok.

title: Independent review findings for the capability slice
description:
PURPOSE

Record a separate reading of the implemented capability slice from the repository, tests and visible system state, without relying on the implementation narrative. This is a review and triage bead: each concern should be resolved, accepted explicitly, or split into a focused follow-up before the capability surface is treated as a security or authority boundary.

VERIFIED PROGRESS

- bin/cap is 762 lines of Python 3.14 standard-library code and remains structurally separate from bin/ms.
- Canonical declarations currently define two roles, three actions and three owned key bindings. Implementations live in a code-owned provider table and action declarations name identifiers rather than arbitrary commands.
- The catalogue distinguishes invalid, unimplemented and runtime-unavailable actions, and reports enforcement=advisory and unattended=false.
- The preview separates binding validity from implementation availability. It reports owned and observed bindings separately, preserves source path, line and raw vendor expression, and attributes package ownership only while live bytes equal the packaged skel bytes.
- The current vendor file contains 75 textual hl.bind calls: 72 resolve statically and 3 are reported unreadable because their keys are computed. No unreadable entry is silently presented as free; matching modifier families report UNKNOWN.
- canonical/desktop/hypr/bindings.lua and the projected live machine-state.lua contain SUPER+M, SUPER+B and SUPER+G bindings derived from the declarations. bin/ms diff reports all targets in sync.
- tests/acceptance.py passes 11/11. tests/cap.py passes 21/21, including five negative controls. Python AST parsing succeeds.

LIMIT OF THIS REVIEW

The current Codex execution environment could read the live projected file but hyprctl reported that Hyprland was not responding. Therefore this review independently verifies declared and projected state, not that the compositor had loaded the bindings or that pressing them performed the action.

FINDINGS TO RESOLVE OR ACCEPT

1. GENERATED CONTENT LIVES UNDER canonical/. canonical/desktop/hypr/bindings.lua says it is generated by cap, while SUBSTRATE.md defines canonical content as human-authored truth. The adapter then treats this generated intermediate as a canonical source for ms. Decide and document its ownership class and whether generated intermediates are permitted under canonical/, or move it to an explicitly derived location without weakening ms source-boundary rules.

2. AGENT PROPOSE-FIRST IS NOT ENFORCED. cmd_act defaults CAP_CALLER to agent and executes immediately; it does not require a preceding proposal or approval token. The catalogue honestly reports advisory enforcement, but descriptions or acceptance claims saying agents propose first are conventions, not current behavior. Keep that distinction explicit until enforcement exists.

3. ROLE DECLARATIONS ARE STILL AN EXECUTION PATH. Actions name provider identifiers, but role.command is agent-writable canonical data and do_ensure passes it through shlex.split to subprocess.Popen. Thus unknown action identifiers cannot execute shell, but changing a role can still select an arbitrary executable and arguments. Decide whether this is intended attended authority, and validate or constrain the command shape accordingly.

4. render DOES NOT APPLY THE UNKNOWN-CHORD SAFEGUARD. cmd_check calls unreadable_risk and rejects chords that may belong to a computed vendor family. cmd_render checks only definite check_chord conflicts and dangling actions. It can therefore render a chord whose correct state is UNKNOWN, then advise ms project; only a later cap check catches it. Rendering and checking should agree about what is safe to project.

5. PROVIDER OUTCOMES CAN OVERSTATE SUCCESS. do_ensure ignores the return code from hyprctl dispatch focuswindow and returns outcome=ok. A rejected or failed focus command can therefore be recorded as successful. The launch branch has the same final-dispatch issue. Provider success must derive from the command result and, ideally, verified post-state.

6. DECLARATION VALIDATION IS UNEVEN. Actions receive explicit validation, while key bindings and roles largely rely on direct indexing and incidental Python or tomllib errors. Missing keys, wrong types, unexpected arguments and malformed binding TOML may produce tracebacks or unclear errors. Invocation parsing also ignores tokens without = and does not validate argument names or types against the action declaration.

7. CTRL AND CONTROL ARE NOT ONE CANONICAL TOKEN. MOD_ORDER assigns both the same sort position, but normalize_chord retains their different spellings. If Hyprland treats them as aliases, CTRL+X and CONTROL+X will evade collision detection. Establish compositor semantics and normalize aliases if appropriate.

8. VENDOR PARSING HAS A DECLARED EVIDENCE LIMIT. It reads single textual lines containing hl.bind and resolves a deliberately small Lua concatenation grammar. It now accounts honestly for all 75 calls in the current file, but this is not a general Lua or runtime-keymap parser and could miss multiline or newly shaped vendor declarations. Keep the claim scoped to the grammar and current input, and ensure future vendor changes fail visibly rather than appearing complete.

9. PROVENANCE WRITING IS NOT CONCURRENCY-SAFE. state/actions.jsonl is appended without locking, durable flush, or handling for a failed write. This may be acceptable at current scale but should be decided before concurrent key, agent and event invocations are introduced.

10. GENERATED BINDINGS EMBED THE ABSOLUTE REPOSITORY PATH. That is valid for a single canonical workstation but makes relocation break every binding. Record this as a deliberate machine-local assumption or derive a stable installed command path.

POSITIVE ARCHITECTURAL READING

The slice demonstrates that roles and bindings compose as data while providers extend behavior as code. Its strongest implemented properties are visible incompleteness, refusal before overwriting the known-good artifact, deterministic generation, explicit evidence limits, and negative controls that prove checks can fail. The next work should preserve those properties while resolving the boundary between generated and canonical state and avoiding claims of enforcement that the code does not yet provide.
acceptance_criteria:
- Every numbered finding is reviewed against the code and classified as fix now, defer with explicit limitation, or accepted design.
- Findings 1, 4 and 5 are resolved before broadening live bindings because they affect ownership or truthfulness of projection and outcomes.
- Any claim that an agent must propose before acting is not presented as enforced until code proves it.
- Live Hyprland behavior is verified from a session where hyprctl can respond, or the verification gap remains explicit.
- Follow-up implementation work is split into focused beads where appropriate; this review bead itself does not authorize unrelated expansion.
notes:
TRIAGE COMPLETE 2026-09-02. All ten findings verified against the code; nine hold as written.

FIXED (8cy.1, .2, .3 — closed, commit 6d5dc96):
  4  render did not apply the UNKNOWN gate check applies. Now refuses, deliberately not warns.
  5  outcomes were assumed. Investigating found worse: 'hyprctl dispatch focuswindow address:X' is a
     syntax error under the Lua config (exit 7), so the focus branch had NEVER worked while
     recording ok. Fixed form, outcome from stdout not exit code, post-state read back, third
     outcome 'unverified'. Compositor facts recorded in canonical/tooling/hypr.md.
  7  PREMISE WAS WRONG, defect was larger. This binary's modifier table has no CTRL. Whether it is
     an alias (missed collision) or invalid (a key that never loads, described as ok), the same fix
     closes it: one accepted spelling per modifier, rejected at load.

OPEN, filed as focused beads:
  1 -> 8cy.4  generated content under canonical/ — DECIDE FIRST, blocks bru.7.5's staging location
  2 -> 8cy.5  propose-first described as behaviour beside code that does not require it
  6 -> 8cy.6  bindings, roles and invocation arguments validated as strictly as actions
  8 -> 8cy.7  the vendor accounting invariant asserted at runtime, not only against a fixture
  3, 9, 10 -> 8cy.8  accepted limitations, to be recorded with their expiry conditions

VERIFICATION GAP FROM THE REVIEW IS CLOSED IN PART: hyprctl responds in this session, so dispatch
behaviour was established empirically. Actual keypress behaviour is still unverified — the fixed
focus path was tested by calling focus_window directly against the active window (no-op) and a
nonexistent address, not by pressing SUPER+M.
VERIFICATION GAP CLOSED 2026-09-02. The review could not reach Hyprland; a real keypress has now been traced end to end.

  declaration   canonical/bindings/keys.toml — SUPER+M -> desktop.application.ensure role=mail
  rendered      canonical/desktop/hypr/bindings.lua
  projected     ~/.config/hypr/config/machine-state.lua:26 (ms diff: in sync)
  LOADED        hyprctl binds shows modmask 64 + M, dispatcher __lua (also B and G)
  invoked       state/actions.jsonl 15:44:55.924Z caller=keypress
  branch        focus — the branch that was broken until 8cy.2
  outcome       ok with NO outcome_detail, so dispatch printed exactly 'ok' AND the
                read-back confirmed the focused window was 0x559f097ec790
  target        that window is class 'Proton Mail', matching role.mail.window_class

Ran under the fixed code: bin/cap modified 15:42:43Z, commit 6d5dc96 at 15:43:47Z, keypress at
15:44:55Z. This is the first journal entry proving the focus branch works. The 15:03:49Z entry
(caller=agent, branch=focus, outcome=ok) predates the fix and is a FALSE ok — the two sit adjacent
in the journal as a before-and-after of the same claim.
close_reason: All ten findings resolved or explicitly accepted, plus 8cy.9 found by a keypress during triage. Nine held as written; finding 7's premise was wrong and the defect was larger. Fixed: render/check disagreement, assumed outcomes (which uncovered that the focus dispatch had never worked), modifier spelling, generated content under canonical/, declaration and invocation validation, the vendor accounting invariant, refusal wording, and the propose-first claim. Accepted with expiry conditions in CAPABILITIES.md 7.1: roles as an execution path, journal concurrency, absolute repo path. Verification gap closed — a real keypress traced end to end with the compositor as independent witness. Test suites grew 14 -> 44 (cap) and 11 -> 13 (acceptance).

title: Deterministic rendering and conflict handling under pressure
description:
THE SHAPES THIS PHASE WORKS WITH ARE NOW KNOWN, not speculative. machine-state-bru.6 produced them
and they are in the repository:

  canonical/roles/roles.toml       [role.<name>] label, command, window_class
  canonical/actions/desktop.toml   [action."<dotted.name>"] label, category, args, mutating, consequence
  canonical/bindings/keys.toml     [[key_binding]] keys, action, args, label

  bin/cap  list --json | propose | act | preview | check | render

  derivation: cap render -> canonical/desktop/hypr/bindings.lua -> ms project -> live key
              cap preview  reads the same declarations
              cap list --json  reads the same declarations

Do not design against the earlier speculative schema. Read the files.

THE QUESTION THIS PHASE ANSWERS: does the coherence model survive composition? The slice proved it
at n=1, which says the idea is real and says nothing about scale. Phase 7 applies scaling pressure
WITHOUT attempting twenty complete integrations — three well-chosen cases that stress different
properties are worth more than twenty of the same shape.

DO NOT PROCEED, from here, to events, unattended grants, or broad provider wrapping. Those are
deferred and the deferral is deliberate.

Two properties that only matter once there is more than one of anything.

DETERMINISM: cap render must produce byte-identical output from identical declarations, regardless
of file order, dict ordering, or how many files the declarations are split across. Non-deterministic
generation would make ms diff report drift that is not drift — and this repository has already been
bitten by a check that reported the wrong thing.

CONFLICT HANDLING AT n>1: the slice proved two kinds of conflict — a chord held by the compositor,
and one chord declared twice by us. With more bindings, also establish:
  - two DIFFERENT actions claiming one chord
  - a chord that becomes conflicted because the vendor claimed it after we declared it, which is
    the case cap check re-reads binds.lua on every run to catch
  - whether render refuses everything or only the conflicted binding, and which is right
acceptance_criteria:
- Identical declarations produce byte-identical rendered output across runs and file splits.
- Two different actions on one chord is reported as a conflict.
- A newly-vendor-claimed chord is caught by cap check without any cache to invalidate.
- The refuse-all versus refuse-one decision is made deliberately and recorded.
notes:
DONE 2026-09-02. tests/cap.py now carries 14 assertions including three negative controls.

A REAL DEFECT FOUND: equivalent modifier orders did not collide. chord_of joined keys in
DECLARATION order, so SUPER + SHIFT + X and SHIFT + SUPER + X were different strings and the
collision was invisible — while the compositor would treat them as one chord. Comparison now runs
on a NORMALISED form: modifiers de-duplicated, sorted into a canonical order, upper-cased, key
last. The declared form is kept for display, since a reader should see what they wrote.

CONFLICT REPORTING now names BOTH claimants with their source file and, where it differs, the form
each was declared in. A conflict that does not say which two declarations conflict leaves the
reader to grep for it.

COORDINATED RENAME SUCCEEDS, which is the other half of the rename semantics. Renaming an action
and every reference together renders cleanly, drops the old identity entirely, and is
deterministic. Partial rename still refuses. Both halves now hold.

THE RACE REPRODUCED AND RECORDED. cap render re-reads vendor state, so it cannot render into a
KNOWN conflict — but nothing prevents the vendor claiming a chord between render and ms project.
Reproduced with a redirected HOME: check passes before, the vendor claims SUPER+M, check fails
after. The precise finding is that the ARTIFACT IS NOT STALE — it still matches its declarations
and check reports it ok. The WORLD changed, not the file. That is why staleness detection cannot
cover this case and why the mitigation belongs in the attended coordinator sketched for
machine-state-bru.7.5: cap render, ms project, then cap check. Detection after the fact, not
prevention.

TWO ASSERTIONS OF MINE WERE WRONG BEFORE THEY WERE RIGHT, both the same mistake: they used the exit
code of cap check while meaning 'no conflict', and cap check now also reports staleness. After
editing declarations without rendering, the artifact IS stale, so both failed for a reason they
were not testing. Fixed by rendering first and asserting on the absence of CONFLICT rather than on
an exit code two mechanisms can set.

THAT LESSON IS NOW A PROJECT INVARIANT, recorded in SUBSTRATE.md section 5: a negative control must
disable exactly the mechanism under test and demonstrate the positive assertion would then miss the
defect. It has been got wrong twice here — once disabling an existence check rather than the
comparison beneath it, once asserting on an exit code two mechanisms could set. Both looked correct
and tested nothing.
close_reason: Chord normalization added after finding equivalent modifier orders did not collide; both claimants now reported with provenance; coordinated rename proven to succeed; the render/project race reproduced and recorded as detection-not-prevention. 14 assertions, three negative controls.

Found and fixed a correctness defect behind the legibility one — the parser read 30 of 75 bindings, so 45 vendor-held chords reported free. Now 72 resolved + 3 declared unreadable, with a third check state (UNKNOWN) for chords whose modifier family matches a computed-key binding. tests/cap.py 21/21 with two new negative controls. title: EVAL: does the two-step workflow hurt under real editing
description:
EVAL: does the two-step workflow (cap render, then ms project) hurt under real editing?

METHOD: make at least six ordinary changes over real use — add a binding, rename a label, change a
role's application, remove a chord. Record how often the second step was forgotten, how it was
noticed, and what it cost.

THE ANSWER IS NOT ONLY A VERDICT. If a coordinator is justified, it must define RECOVERY, not just
detection. bru.7.3 proved the render/project race is detected and not prevented; a coordinator that
only detects it more promptly adds a step without adding safety. The sequence it must implement:

  1. capture the vendor fingerprint
  2. render into staging
  3. confirm the vendor fingerprint is unchanged
  4. project
  5. post-check
  6. on failure: roll back, or raise visibly

Steps 3 and 6 are the ones that make it a coordinator rather than a convenience script.

QUESTIONS THE EVAL MUST ANSWER, not the implementation:
  - Is failure unmistakable, or can a half-applied projection look like success?
  - Does recovery restore the previous known-good projection, or merely stop?
  - Can it disable only the newly introduced binding, leaving the rest live?
  - Or is detection-with-manual-recovery explicitly accepted for v1, and recorded as accepted?

The last option is legitimate. What is not legitimate is leaving it undecided.

KEEP THE BOUNDARY: cap render then ms project is architecturally correct — semantic declarations to
projected source, then projected source to the live machine. A coordinator composes the two tools;
it must not merge them. Do not build it before the eval says the friction is real.
acceptance_criteria:
- At least six ordinary editing changes made over real use, with the second step's cost recorded.
- A count of how often ms project was forgotten and how it was noticed.
- A recorded verdict: immaterial, or build the coordinator.
- If a coordinator is justified, the recovery behaviour is specified before any code: rollback
  versus visible failure, whole-projection versus single-binding, decided rather than discovered.
- If detection-with-manual-recovery is accepted for v1, that acceptance is recorded explicitly.
notes:
STAGING LOCATION ANSWERED by 8cy.4 (2026-09-02). derived/ is now an ownership class of its own: produced here by a tool from canonical declarations, read by ms, never written by ms. bin/ms enforces that an adapter source must be under canonical/ or derived/, at manifest load, so every command checks it.

So a coordinator stages under derived/. It does not need ms's source rules widened, and it must not stage anywhere else — a source outside those two roots is now refused with exit 2.
EVAL RUN 2026-09-02. Six ordinary editing changes, each measured at three stages: (A) declaration edited and nothing run, (B) cap render run but ms project not, (C) both run. Baseline captured and restored byte-for-byte afterwards; the live projected file is identical to before the trial.

  change                          two-step needed?   A: cap check / ms diff   B: cap check / ms diff
  1 add a chord                   YES                FAIL / "in sync"          clean / FAIL
  2 rename a label                no                 clean / clean            clean / clean
  3 change a role's command       no                 clean / clean            clean / clean
  4 remove a chord                YES                FAIL / "in sync"          clean / FAIL
  5 add a role, no binding        no                 clean / clean            clean / clean
  6 change a chord's args         YES                FAIL / "in sync"          clean / FAIL

FINDING 1 — THE TWO-STEP APPLIES TO FEWER EDITS THAN ASSUMED. The derived artifact is a thin index:
it carries chord -> action name + args and nothing else. Labels, role commands, window classes,
categories and consequence classes all resolve at invocation time. Only a change to a CHORD or to
what a chord invokes needs render and project. Three of six ordinary edits; the other three take
effect immediately with no second step to forget.

FINDING 2 — THE PROBLEM IS NOT UNDETECTED FAILURE, IT IS FALSE ASSURANCE. For the three that do
need it, the pattern is invariant: whichever step is outstanding, the OTHER tool reports success.
Edit a declaration and ms diff says 'all targets match canonical'. Render without projecting and cap
check says everything is ok. Neither tool ever reports both, so there is no single command that
answers 'is the machine current with my declarations?' — and asking the wrong one returns a
confident, wrong yes.

That is worse than a silent gap. A missing signal invites checking; a reassuring one does not.

VERDICT: BUILD THE COORDINATOR, but the evidence supports a smaller one than the bead assumed. The
forgetting problem needs a combined STATUS, not orchestration. The race needs the fingerprint
sequence. Both fit in one thin attended tool that sequences cap and ms as subprocesses and holds no
logic of its own.
close_reason: Eval run: six changes, three stages each, baseline restored byte-for-byte. Three of six need the two-step; for those, whichever step is outstanding the OTHER tool reports success — false assurance, not silence. Verdict: build a thin coordinator. bin/machine status asks both; machine apply runs fingerprint/render/confirm/project/post-check with whole-artifact rollback. Per-binding disable rejected deliberately and recorded. 11/11 tests with three negative controls. Also produced the projection-record identity guard after the new test unprojected the live workstation.

title: Phase 7: does the coherence model survive composition
description:
SHARED CONTEXT (true for every bead in this epic)

THE CLAIM version one must prove: the human, desktop and agent all operate from the same model of
the machine. Every surface tells the same truth. Nothing here is about adding AI features.

A HARD CONSTRAINT: removing the agent must still leave a coherent, fully usable workstation.
Agent-first means the machine is arranged to collaborate with agents, not that ordinary operation
collapses without one.

Read SUBSTRATE.md and CAPABILITIES.md first; they are the contract. Python 3.14 stdlib only, no new
runtime. Never root, never sudo, no network. dcg guards the shell beneath everything. Task tracking
is bd; bd human is the escalation channel. Every check must be proven able to FAIL, not merely to
pass — see SUBSTRATE.md section 5.

The tool is a PEER to bin/ms and must never be folded into it. ms governs durable projection and
drift; this governs runtime action. Declarations here are canonical state projected BY ms.

THEME IS OUT OF SCOPE. Noctalia already is the semantic theme registry: builtin_ids for btop, gtk3,
gtk4, kcolorscheme, kitty, qt and alacritty; wallpaper_scheme m3-tonal-spot; 54 template adapters;
colour-scheme and theme-mode commands at runtime. Reference it, never rebuild it.

The cohesion work, folded into this epic rather than deferred to a sibling, because the claim
version one must prove IS cohesion. A capability layer with no shared vocabulary would satisfy none
of the product test.

Four canonical registries were proposed; three are in scope. Theme is not, because Noctalia already
provides it.

  roles        which application fulfils a role: mail, browser, terminal, editor
  actions      what the workstation can do, named semantically
  bindings     how humans, agents and events invoke actions

From these, three things are DERIVED rather than separately maintained: the live Hyprland key
binding, the shortcut preview row, and the agent-readable action listing. That derivation is the
whole point. A preview that can disagree with reality is worse than no preview.
design:
THE LIFECYCLE ASSERTIONS phase 7 must establish. These are the revealing ones — several are
sharper than the phase's original wording and replace it:

  1. Removing a declaration removes every derived surface AND NOTHING ELSE.
  2. Renaming an action leaves no stale old identifier anywhere.
  3. A FAILED RENDER PRESERVES THE LAST VALID GENERATED STATE.
  4. Repeated renders are byte-identical.
  5. Multiple bindings to one action remain unambiguous.
  6. A vendor collision refuses BEFORE producing partial output.
  7. Human preview and agent catalogue remain CONSISTENT WHILE PRESENTING DIFFERENT INFORMATION.
     Consistent is not identical: they serve different readers and must not diverge in truth.
  8. cap check detects manually altered or stale generated artifacts, not only chord conflicts.
  9. THE SYSTEM REMAINS USABLE IF THE AGENT INTERFACE IS ABSENT. This is the product test's hardest
     constraint expressed as an assertion: the keys, the preview and the applications must work
     with no agent present at all.

Assertions 3 and 6 are about atomicity and ordering: refusing must happen before writing, and a
refusal must not leave the machine worse than it found it. Assertion 9 is the one that keeps this
from becoming a machine that only works when a model provider is reachable.

WHAT bru.7.1 IS ACTUALLY FOR: not a generalised schema. Evidence about which parts of the
provisional shapes remain stable once a second and third case arrive. Expect some to move.

CADENCE: prove at n=1, stress composition, revise abstractions, widen only what survived. Do not
reopen phases 1 to 4 until the phase 7 evaluation records its findings.
notes:
EXTENSIBILITY RULE ADOPTED 2026-09-02, from a design review, and implemented:

  new role                data only
  new binding             data only
  existing action reused  data only
  new semantic behaviour  provider code

Declarations compose the system; implementations extend its abilities. That asymmetry is what keeps
the registry a protocol rather than a configuration-shaped programming language.

THREE STATES, now independent facts in the catalogue rather than one flag:
  invalid        the declaration is malformed — REJECTED, naming file and problem, exit 2
  unimplemented  a valid action no provider implements — kept, shown with !, reason given
  unavailable    implemented but its runtime dependency is absent — shown with the concrete reason

  { declared: true, implemented: false, available: false, reason: "..." }

IMPLEMENTATION IS AN IDENTIFIER, NEVER A COMMAND. An action declares
implementation = "desktop.application.ensure" and code owns the dispatch table. An unknown
identifier is unimplemented: it is never executed as a shell command and never silently omitted.
That is the property that stops the registry becoming an execution path.

BINDINGS TO UNIMPLEMENTED ACTIONS RENDER, deliberately choosing the second of the two coherent
options. SUPER+G is declared against an unimplemented action; the key is rendered, the preview shows
it with its reason, and pressing it produces a desktop notification saying the action is
unavailable — rather than appearing to do nothing. Binding, preview and catalogue keep agreeing, and
a declaration may precede its implementation without presenting false capability. Provenance records
outcome refused with caller keypress.

A BUG THIS SURFACED: cmd_preview still referenced the removed IMPL table and crashed with
NameError once the provider table replaced it. The traceback was hidden because the failing rows
came after the header, so the view looked merely empty rather than broken — a reminder that a
partially-rendered surface can read as an empty one.
close_reason: All five children closed. The coherence model survives composition: n=3 with an unbound action and two chords on one action (7.1); lifecycle add/remove/rename/invalid/stale (7.2); conflict pressure, chord normalisation and determinism (7.3); vendor rows as evidence, which uncovered that 45 of 75 vendor chords read as free (7.4); and the two-step eval, which produced bin/machine (7.5). Independent review folded in as machine-state-8cy, ten findings resolved or accepted. Suites: acceptance 15, cap 44, machine 11 — all with negative controls that are now proven to disable something.

title: Expand to n=3, choosing cases that stress different properties
description:
THE SHAPES THIS PHASE WORKS WITH ARE NOW KNOWN, not speculative. machine-state-bru.6 produced them
and they are in the repository:

  canonical/roles/roles.toml       [role.<name>] label, command, window_class
  canonical/actions/desktop.toml   [action."<dotted.name>"] label, category, args, mutating, consequence
  canonical/bindings/keys.toml     [[key_binding]] keys, action, args, label

  bin/cap  list --json | propose | act | preview | check | render

  derivation: cap render -> canonical/desktop/hypr/bindings.lua -> ms project -> live key
              cap preview  reads the same declarations
              cap list --json  reads the same declarations

Do not design against the earlier speculative schema. Read the files.

THE QUESTION THIS PHASE ANSWERS: does the coherence model survive composition? The slice proved it
at n=1, which says the idea is real and says nothing about scale. Phase 7 applies scaling pressure
WITHOUT attempting twenty complete integrations — three well-chosen cases that stress different
properties are worth more than twenty of the same shape.

DO NOT PROCEED, from here, to events, unattended grants, or broad provider wrapping. Those are
deferred and the deferral is deliberate.

Three additions, each chosen because it stresses something the slice could not:

  1. ANOTHER APPLICATION ROLE — does a second role compose, or did the first one work because it
     was alone? Choose one already installed and resolvable; firefox is present with class firefox,
     and kitty is present with class kitty.

  2. AN ACTION WITHOUT A KEY BINDING — the registries are separate objects, so an action with no
     chord must be fully usable by an agent and must simply not appear as a key. If it cannot
     exist without a binding, the separation is nominal.

  3. TWO BINDINGS TARGETING ONE ACTION WITH DIFFERENT ARGUMENTS — for example two chords, both
     desktop.application.ensure, with different roles. This is the case that tests whether the
     action is genuinely an identity rather than a synonym for one binding.

n=3 is the target, not n=20. The point is coverage of shapes, not volume.
acceptance_criteria:
- A second role resolves and is usable through the same action.
- An action with no key binding is present in the agent catalogue and absent from the key surface.
- Two chords invoke one action with different arguments, and the preview shows both.
- No change to bin/cap is required for any of these, or the reason it was required is recorded.
notes:
DONE 2026-09-02. n=3 reached: roles mail and browser; actions desktop.application.ensure and
desktop.window.list; chords SUPER+M and SUPER+B both invoking ensure with different roles.

EVIDENCE, which is the point of this bead rather than the schema:

WHAT NEEDED NO CODE. A second role and a second chord were purely declarative — added to TOML,
worked immediately, cap check passed, both rendered. The role and key-binding shapes survive
composition unchanged.

WHAT NEEDED CODE, and this is the finding. Adding an ACTION required an entry in the IMPL table in
bin/cap, because implementations are Python functions while declarations are data. So the registry
is not fully declarative and adding an action is not the same kind of act as adding a role or a
binding. The catalogue now says so honestly: an action with no implementation lists as unavailable
with a reason. Whether that asymmetry is acceptable or should be closed is a real design question
this bead surfaced and does not settle.

A DEFECT THAT ONLY APPEARS AT n>1, which is exactly what composition pressure is for. The preview
preferred the ACTION's label over the BINDING's. At n=1 that was invisible. At n=2 both chords
rendered as 'Open or focus an application' and a reader could not tell SUPER+M from SUPER+B —
assertion 5, multiple bindings to one action remain unambiguous, was failing. Fixed: the binding
label wins, falling back to the action label. The action label names the operation; the binding
label says what THIS chord does.

CONTRACT REFINED BY THE OBSERVE CASE. query/propose/act binds MUTATING actions: propose exists so a
change can be reviewed before it happens. desktop.window.list changes nothing, so demanding a
proposal would be ceremony rather than safety. Its propose reports 'reads N windows; changes
nothing'.

SEPARATION CONFIRMED REAL, NOT NOMINAL. desktop.window.list is fully usable by an agent and appears
on zero key surfaces. An action can exist without a chord.

ASSERTIONS ESTABLISHED WHILE HERE:
  4. repeated renders byte-identical — three consecutive renders, same sha
  3. a failed render preserves the last valid state — pointing a chord at SUPER+E made render exit
     1 and left the generated file byte-unchanged, so refusal happens before writing
  6. a vendor collision refuses before producing partial output — same test, same evidence
close_reason: n=3 reached. Roles and bindings compose with no code; actions require an IMPL entry, so the registry is not fully declarative — recorded as an open design question. A label-precedence defect invisible at n=1 broke assertion 5 at n=2 and is fixed. Assertions 3, 4 and 6 established in passing.

title: Lifecycle: the output boundary must be as strict as the input boundary
description:
The loader boundary is proven: invalid input is rejected, and a duplicate key was caught on its first day. This bead makes the OUTPUT boundary equally strict — failed derivation must leave the last coherent truth intact.

THE GOVERNING RULE, from a failure that already happened here:

  A generated or queried surface must be COMPLETE, or VISIBLY FAIL. It must never resemble a valid
  empty surface.

cmd_preview once referenced a table that had been replaced, and crashed after writing its header.
The view read as EMPTY rather than BROKEN, which is the worse of the two: a reader concludes there
is nothing rather than that something is wrong.

ALREADY DONE, ahead of this bead, because the misreading was live:
  - the preview is built completely in memory before anything is printed
  - on internal failure it emits NO normal output, a clear stderr message, and exits non-zero
  - proven by negative control: a stale reference inside preview produces 0 stdout lines, a
    NameError on stderr, and exit 1, while a catalogue with no owned bindings prints normally and
    exits 0. Broken and empty are distinguishable.
  - binding validity and action executability are now separate columns, because a single ok
    spanning both reads as availability when only the chord is sound

REMAINING FOR THIS BEAD:
  - generate artifacts in staging and validate them BEFORE replacing good output
  - preserve previous known-good artifacts when rendering fails (partly established: a vendor
    collision already leaves the generated file byte-unchanged)
  - remove artifacts corresponding to DELETED declarations, and nothing else
  - remove old identities after a RENAME, leaving no stale identifier anywhere
  - detect stale or mixed-generation artifacts, not only chord conflicts
  - ensure competing declarations produce no partial update
  - repeated rendering yields the same bytes (established at n=3; re-establish under these changes)
  - a negative control recreating the stale-reference failure, kept in the test suite

MULTI-FILE TRANSACTIONALITY, to be decided consciously rather than deferred by accident. Atomic
replacement makes ONE file safe; it cannot make a SET transactional. An interruption between two
writes leaves a mixed generation that every individual file passes.

  Decision now: one generated artifact exists, so atomic replace is sufficient and a manifest would
  be machinery for a problem that does not exist. THE TRIGGER IS THE SECOND GENERATED FILE, not a
  future date. At that point each artifact carries a generation identifier, or a manifest records
  the hashes for one generation, so cap check can detect a mixed set after interruption.

  Record which was chosen and why when the trigger fires.
acceptance_criteria:
- Rendering writes to staging, validates, then replaces; a failure leaves the previous artifact byte-identical.
- A deleted declaration removes its derived artifact and nothing else.
- A renamed action leaves no stale identifier in any generated or queried surface.
- Stale or mixed-generation artifacts are detected by cap check.
- Repeated renders are byte-identical.
- Broken and empty surfaces are distinguishable, with a negative control in the test suite.
- The multi-file transactionality decision is recorded, with its trigger stated.
notes:
DONE 2026-09-02. All six lifecycle cases pass, two of them only after fixing real defects.

  add     -> appears
  remove  -> disappears, and nothing else does
  rename  -> render REFUSES; no stale identity reaches the artifact
  invalid -> the previous good artifact survives byte-for-byte
  stale   -> cap check fails and names the artifact
  same in -> same bytes out

WHAT WAS ALREADY CORRECT: add, remove and determinism. Removal was initially reported broken and
was not — the test's own edit had truncated two bindings instead of one. Worth recording because
the first evidence was wrong and the code was right.

TWO REAL DEFECTS, both in the rename and stale cases:

  1. render did not refuse a DANGLING reference. Renaming an action left every binding pointing at
     nothing, and render happily baked the stale identity into the artifact. The key would then
     call an action that could not be found — and worse, cap act died with exit 2 rather than
     taking the refusal path, so a keypress produced no notification and no explanation. Both
     fixed: render refuses before writing, and an unknown action now refuses gracefully with its
     notification and a provenance record.

  2. cap check never looked at ARTIFACTS, only chords. It now checks three distinct things because
     three distinct things can be wrong: a chord can be taken, a binding can point at a missing
     action, and the generated file can no longer match what the declarations would produce —
     stale, hand-edited, or left from an interrupted render.

STALE DETECTION CAUGHT A REAL STALENESS ON ITS FIRST RUN. Making render_text pure changed the
output for a binding with no args, so the on-disk artifact no longer matched. The check reported it
immediately rather than the difference surviving unnoticed.

tests/cap.py added, 8 assertions, hermetic, and wired into the pre-push hook alongside the ms
acceptance suite. Two negative controls, and the first attempt at one was itself wrong: disabling
the stale check by replacing 'if RENDERED.exists()' fell through to the elif that reports a MISSING
artifact, so a problem was still raised and the control tested nothing. It now disables the
comparison itself. A negative control that does not disable the mechanism it claims to is worse
than none.
close_reason: Six lifecycle cases pass. Two real defects found and fixed: render did not refuse dangling action references, and cap check never inspected artifacts. tests/cap.py added with two negative controls and wired into the pre-push hook.

title: Emit on every path, including failure
description:
SHARED CONTEXT (true for every bead in this epic)

The tool is a PEER to bin/ms and must never be folded into it. ms governs durable projection and
drift; this governs runtime capabilities and actions. Folding them gives the projector a runtime
and the runtime the projector's write access. Read SUBSTRATE.md and CAPABILITIES.md in this
repository before starting; they are the contract, not background reading.

Constraints that apply throughout:
- Python 3.14 standard library only. No pip, no venv, no new runtime. This machine has no node,
  go or rust toolchain and is not to acquire one.
- Never root, never sudo, no network, no git invocation.
- dcg guards the shell beneath everything. A refusal is answered by narrowing the command, never
  by disabling the guard.
- Every check must be proven able to FAIL, not merely to pass. See SUBSTRATE.md section 5. A
  check that cannot fail reports green for the wrong reason; that has already happened twice in
  this repository.
- Task tracking is bd. Do not use markdown TODO lists. bd human is the escalation channel.
- Consequence classes are observe, report, adjust, commit. Defined in CAPABILITIES.md section 4.

The record is only worth having if nothing escapes it.

Every exit path from an invocation must emit: success, refusal by consequence class, failure of the
underlying command, timeout, and escalation. A capability that fails silently and leaves no record
is worse than one that fails loudly, because the corpus then contains a gap that looks like
absence of activity.

A PARTIAL RECORD IS WORSE THAN NONE FOR ANALYSIS, and this repository has a live example: the dcg

propose and ms project are exactly this decomposition for projection, and propose earned its place
immediately by exposing a real defect that ms diff had been hiding.

- query: read state, change nothing
- propose: compute and return what would change, change nothing
- act: perform it

that can only act. This is a CONTRACT, not an option some capabilities offer.

three related capabilities? How does the registry express that propose and act correspond? What
does propose return for a capability whose effect cannot be predicted without doing it, and is such
a capability allowed at all?

- A mutating capability without a propose level is rejected, or the reason it is exempt is recorded.

- description, one line, written for a reader who has not seen the code
- inputs and outputs, with types
- availability: what must be installed or running for this to work at all
- read-only versus mutating
- consequence class: observe, report, adjust or commit

declaration files here.

title: Grants: put the authority boundary somewhere an agent cannot reach
description:
CAPABILITIES.md section 8 called this the open question everything else rests on. canonical/ is agent-writable by design — that is the point of ms project — so grants deciding what may run unattended cannot live there, or an agent widens its own authority.

WHAT WAS ESTABLISHED FIRST, 2026-09-02, because the answer depends on which boundaries are real:

  everything in HOME is agent-writable, including dcg's own config. A write setting
  fail_closed = false to ~/.config/dcg/config.toml tests as ALLOWED. So the earlier claim that
  not projecting dcg's config kept it out of the substrate's reach was WRONG — that was a
  convention, never a boundary, and it is corrected in the record.

  dcg does not block sudo either; that command tests as ALLOWED. The barrier is the password.

  sudo -n true exits 1: a password is required. Root IS a boundary, and it is the only one
  available on this machine without new machinery.

  dcg's own config layering cannot help: system /etc/dcg/config.toml is the LOWEST priority
  layer, so a user-writable ~/.config/dcg/config.toml overrides it. Only the project-level
  .dcg.toml is enforcement-only, and that lives in the agent-writable repo.

DECISION: grants live at /etc/machine-state/grants.toml, root-owned, agent-readable,
agent-unwritable. The containing directory must be root-owned too — deleting a file needs write
permission on its DIRECTORY, not the file, so a user-writable directory would leave the boundary
only half there.

Fail-closed: absent or unreadable grants means nothing runs unattended. The safe initial state is
therefore no grants at all, which is also the honest one.

THE SUBSTRATE MUST VERIFY ITS OWN BOUNDARY. ms status reports whether grants are intact and exits
non-zero if the file or its directory has become writable by this user. A boundary that cannot
report its own compromise is not one.
acceptance_criteria:
- Grants live at a root-owned path; the directory is root-owned so the file cannot be deleted.
- ms status reports the boundary state and exits non-zero when it is compromised.
- The check is proven able to fail, not merely to pass.
- Fail-closed: no grants means nothing runs unattended.
- The corrected claim about dcg's config being a convention rather than a boundary is recorded.
notes:
DELIVERED 2026-09-02, up to the sudo step, which is the user's by design.

grants_state() in bin/ms checks both the file AND its directory, and ms status grows a Boundary
section that exits non-zero when the boundary is compromised.

PROVEN FALSIFIABLE, and the first attempt at proving it was inadequate. All four states produced
the right label but every one exited 1, because the scratch copy also reports codex UNGUARDED,
which fails independently. The exit code could not discriminate. Re-tested by matching the stderr
message instead:

  /etc/machine-state absent          -> boundary ok, fails only on the unguarded harness
  root-owned dir and file present    -> boundary ok, fails only on the unguarded harness
  user-writable directory            -> fails ON THE BOUNDARY

A CORRECTION THIS FORCED. This record previously implied that not projecting ~/.config/dcg/config.toml
kept it beyond the substrate's reach. That was wrong and is now corrected in canonical/tooling/dcg.md.
Not projecting a file keeps ms out of it; it does not keep an agent out of it. The file is
klaas:klaas 644 and a write setting fail_closed = false tests as ALLOWED — dcg does not guard its
own configuration. It was a convention against systematic weakening, never a boundary against
deliberate weakening.

The initial grants.toml is generated and valid, containing no grants. That is the correct initial
state rather than a placeholder: fail-closed means nothing runs unattended until something outside
the agent's reach says otherwise.

STRICTNESS, recorded 2026-09-02 rather than built. The first grants file is one root-owned file,
all or nothing — the right starting point and the wrong ending one. Three properties are worth
taking from dcg when the broker exists, and the current schema forecloses none of them; each is
additive.

Enforcement-only layering is the sharpest. dcg's project layer can tighten but never loosen, which
is the one shape provably safe to hand an agent. Applied to grants: a root-owned baseline, plus a
higher agent-writable layer that may only REDUCE what is granted. That buys something genuinely
useful — an agent can voluntarily drop its own authority for a risky task and cannot raise it.
Self-restriction is safe to delegate; self-permission is not.

Modes, for staged introduction: a grant begins as warn, recording what it would have done, promoted
only once the log justifies it. Exactly how the four dcg packs were introduced here.

Expiry: a permission granted once should not be permanent by default. It is the difference between
a decision and a sediment.

NOT borrowed yet, deliberately: graduated response, pattern packs, allowlist machinery. Those
earned their complexity from a large rule surface. Grants currently number zero.

title: ms propose: a review seam between canonical and the machine
description:
Today an agent edits canonical/ directly and runs ms project. There is no step where a change is described, diffed and reviewed BEFORE it becomes authoritative. That is the gap an external architecture review named, and it is the same seam the authority problem opens at: canonical is agent-writable by design, so an agent can edit its own operating rules — or, later, its own grants — and project them.

A second, related defect makes this concrete. ms diff cannot currently distinguish two different situations, and reports both as 'drifted':

  the target was hand-edited                  -> reality diverged, canonical should win
  canonical was edited and not yet projected  -> canonical moved ahead, projecting will apply it

These want opposite responses, and the data to tell them apart is already stored: state/projection.json records the sha we last wrote. Target matching that sha but not current canonical means canonical moved. Target matching neither means it was edited.

WHAT ms propose DOES: shows exactly what ms project would change, without changing anything, annotated with the cause of each change and a line-level summary. Exit non-zero when anything is pending, so it is scriptable as 'is there an unapplied change'.

WHAT IT DOES NOT DO, and this must be recorded rather than implied: propose is a REVIEW seam, not ENFORCEMENT. It makes a change visible before it lands. It does not prevent an agent from editing canonical and running project anyway. Enforcement needs the grants mechanism in CAPABILITIES.md section 8, which is unresolved.
acceptance_criteria:
- ms propose reports what ms project would do and changes nothing.
- Each pending change is annotated with its cause: canonical moved ahead, target edited, or new.
- Exit non-zero when changes are pending, zero when clean.
- ms diff gains the same cause annotation, so drift and pending-projection are no longer conflated.
- The review-not-enforcement limit is stated in the record.
notes:
DELIVERED 2026-09-01. ms propose added; ms diff gains the same cause annotation.

The conflation was verified before it was fixed: editing a shared canonical fragment and editing a
target both produced the identical line, 'drifted ... (region differs)'. Now:

  canonical moved ahead - this is our own unapplied change    (+2 -0 lines, BOTH files)
  target changed since we wrote it                            (+0 -1 lines, one file)

The extent is worth having on its own. A canonical edit to a shared fragment shows up on every
target that selects it, while a target edit shows up on exactly one — which is itself a signal the
tool previously threw away.

Implementation is small: cause() compares the target against the hash already recorded in
state/projection.json, and line_delta() uses difflib. No new state, no new mechanism.

LIMIT RECORDED in SUBSTRATE.md section 5 as well as here: propose is review, not enforcement. It
makes a change visible before it reaches the machine. It cannot stop an agent editing canonical and
running project anyway, because canonical is agent-writable by design. Closing that needs the grants
mechanism in CAPABILITIES.md section 8.
close_reason: ms propose implemented with cause annotation and line extent; ms diff no longer conflates canonical-moved with target-edited. Review seam only; enforcement still needs the grants mechanism.

title: Agent-native workstation: agents as operators of the OS, not applications
description:
PURPOSE

Express the guiding intent of machine-state: this laptop should have CachyOS deeply integrated into agentic workflows. Resident agents should operate as a policy-governed layer over the OS and user session, rather than merely appearing as desktop applications.

The envisioned layer includes Hyprland window and workspace control, application integration such as Proton Mail triage, notifications and user services, and future agent-neutral capabilities for observing and acting on the workstation. The substrate should keep canonical policy, adapters, safety boundaries, permissions, provenance, and auditability independent of any one agent harness.

This differs from an approach such as Omarchy where agents are integrated primarily as applications: here, agents are intended to become controlled operators of the desktop environment and operating system.

SAMPLE STATUS

This is intentionally also a sample bead created to test that Codex can use the repository's Beads workflow correctly. It may later be refined, promoted into an epic, or closed once the intent has been captured elsewhere.
acceptance_criteria:
- The issue clearly records the agent-native workstation vision.
- It distinguishes an OS control layer from agents delivered merely as applications.
- It names representative capabilities: Hyprland control and Proton Mail triage.
- It explicitly records that this is a sample bead used to test Codex integration.

title: Choose a safe Proton Mail access route for agents
description:
Recorded 2026-09-01 while setting up mail, so the reasoning is not lost between now and when triage becomes real.

GOAL: the resident agent assists with email triage on this machine.

The desktop app (proton-mail-bin) cannot serve this. Proton Mail is end-to-end encrypted, so plaintext exists only inside a client holding the keys, and the app is a sealed Electron GUI with no local API. Screen automation is the only route through it and is not worth having.

THREE ROUTES, in the order they were considered:
1. Proton Mail Bridge — decrypts locally, exposes IMAP/SMTP on 127.0.0.1. Reachable with Python stdlib imaplib, so an agent tool needs no dependencies. Costs a persistent systemd --user service, a Secret Service daemon, and a generated IMAP password to hold.
2. Proton's own client libraries — Bridge is built on them, so this is the layer beneath the IMAP hop rather than a parallel one. Skips the service, the IMAP translation, and arguably the credential-in-a-mail-protocol problem.
3. An existing Proton MCP server, if one is maintained and trustworthy.

PREFERENCE (user, 2026-09-01): route 2 or 3 over Bridge. Verify what Proton actually publishes and what state it is in before committing — this preference was recorded from memory, not from reading the repositories.

CONSEQUENCE FOR THE MAIL SETUP: the client choice does NOT constrain the agent side. Installing the desktop app now forecloses nothing, and Bridge does not need to be installed 'so the agent can have mail later'.

CONSEQUENCE FOR THE SUBSTRATE: whichever route wins, the agent needs a credential. SUBSTRATE.md section 9 lists 'no secrets management' as a deliberate non-goal. That question must be answered BEFORE writing anything that reads mail, not after. This is the bead that will force it.
acceptance_criteria:
- Established what Proton actually publishes and whether a maintained MCP server exists.
- A route chosen, with the secrets question answered first.
- Nothing that reads mail is written before that answer exists.
notes: CURRENT OPTIONS, researched 2026-09-03. No official Proton MCP or supported consumer Mail API was found. Proton officially supports Mail Bridge on Linux; it decrypts locally and exposes loopback IMAP/SMTP, requires a paid Mail plan and a Secret Service keyring, and publishes an Arch-compatible PKGBUILD while officially supporting Ubuntu LTS and Fedora. COMMUNITY ROUTE A: fbossiere/proton-safe-mcp uses official Bridge, local STDIO, read/search plus draft creation, and structurally omits send/delete/move; it supports separate terminal approval and stores only the Bridge-generated local password in the OS keyring. This is the strongest existing candidate for an attended first experiment, subject to source/dependency review. COMMUNITY ROUTE B: several broader Bridge MCPs expose send, move and delete; these have a materially larger prompt-injection blast radius and should not be the starting point. DIRECT ROUTE: filippofinke/protonmail-rs provides an unofficial Rust client, CLI and 56-tool MCP using direct Proton APIs and Proton Rust crypto crates, but handles the full auth/key/decryption surface, masquerades as official client types, and explicitly lacks Key Transparency verification. Proton's official go-proton-api library is actively used by Proton clients and tools, but wrapping it ourselves means owning authentication, key handling, API compatibility and an MCP safety layer. RECOMMENDATION TO EVALUATE, not yet chosen: first audit or reproduce the narrow Bridge-backed design with read-only tools, then optionally draft-only output with out-of-band human approval. Never expose send/delete/move in the initial capability set. Resolve the substrate secrets/credential-lease question before installing or connecting any route.

comments.author: root-mechanicum
comments.text:
ORDERING CONSTRAINT, noticed 2026-09-02 while planning the capability layer (machine-state-bru).

A proposed extension manifest for a Proton provider reads, in part:

  id      = "proton.mail"
  secrets = ["proton.session"]

SUBSTRATE.md section 9 lists secrets management as an explicit non-goal. So Proton is the first
provider that collides with it, and the collision is structural rather than incidental: every route
to agent access — Bridge IMAP, Proton's client libraries, an MCP server — needs a credential the
agent can reach.

The constraint this creates: the secrets non-goal must be revisited BEFORE a Proton provider is
built, not discovered during. Deciding how a capability obtains a credential, and what a credential
lease looks like, is a prerequisite rather than an implementation detail.

Note also that the capability layer makes this sharper, not softer. A capability that reads mail
would be report class at best, and its provenance record would name the credential it used. Both
are good, and both presume a secrets model that does not exist yet.

comments.author: root-mechanicum
comments.text: PROVISIONAL DIRECTION, user decision 2026-09-03: pencil in the official Proton Mail Bridge plus a basic local MCP for the proof of concept. Begin with a deliberately small read-only surface: list folders/inbox, search, read a selected message or thread, and inspect bounded text from selected attachments if needed. Use local STDIO, loopback Bridge IMAP, and the Bridge-generated credential held in the OS keyring. Do not initially expose SMTP/send, delete, move, filters, labels, account settings, or raw filesystem attachment access. Draft creation can be considered later only if the read-only experiment is useful and an attended approval path is designed. The direct go-proton-api/Rust idea was exploratory only and creates no planned implementation work.

comments.author: root-mechanicum
comments.text:
PROVIDER-NEUTRAL MAIL MCP DESIGN, recorded 2026-09-03.

The proof of concept should be a provider-neutral Mail MCP, not a Proton-specific MCP. Proton Mail Bridge over loopback IMAP is the first provider because it is the smallest practical route, but the provider boundary must allow later replacement by go-proton-api or addition of Gmail and generic IMAP without changing agent-facing tools.

LAYERS:
  MCP tools
    -> shared mail domain and safety policy
    -> provider interface
    -> Proton Bridge/IMAP | Proton native API | Gmail API | generic IMAP

INITIAL READ-ONLY TOOLS:
  mail.accounts
  mail.list
  mail.search
  mail.read
  mail.read_thread
  mail.list_attachments

Draft creation may later appear as mail.propose_draft. Sending, deletion, movement, filters, labels, account administration, and other mutations are excluded initially.

SHARED MODEL:
  Account, MessageSummary, Message, Thread, AttachmentMetadata, MailboxQuery, ProviderCapabilities, MailError.

Provider-native identifiers remain opaque metadata and never become the stable MCP identity. Normalize conservatively: Gmail labels are not IMAP folders, and Proton conversations are not necessarily Gmail threads. Providers advertise capabilities rather than pretending semantic parity. Genuine provider-only behavior belongs in optional namespaced extensions.

ACCOUNT ROLES:
Agents address semantic roles such as personal, work, and notifications. A registry resolves a role to its current provider and credentials. Changing personal from Proton Bridge to Proton native API, or to Gmail, must not change the agent-facing request.

SECURITY:
Email is hostile external input. The shared mail layer owns safety: read-only default; message content always marked untrusted; instructions inside mail never treated as user instructions; bounded body and attachment extraction; no raw attachment paths or unrestricted filesystem access; credentials hidden behind the provider boundary; explicit approval for draft creation; a separate stronger authority for sending if ever added; provenance records the account role, provider, initiating request, and result.

FIRST IMPLEMENTATION:
Official Proton Mail Bridge, loopback IMAP, local STDIO MCP, Bridge-generated credential in the OS keyring, and the narrow read-only tool set. Provider contract tests define observable behavior. A future Proton native or Gmail adapter must pass the same contract tests before joining or replacing Bridge.

SEQUENCE:
1. Implement the shared read-only contract.
2. Add the Proton Bridge provider.
3. Validate real triage and search use cases.
4. Refine the shared model from observed provider semantics.
5. Optionally add proposed drafts with attended approval.
6. Add Gmail only when a real account/use case exists.
7. Re-evaluate a native Proton provider after roughly six months.
8. Add send or destructive actions only behind a separately designed authority model.

The durable abstraction is mail.read, not IMAP, Gmail, Proton Bridge, or go-proton-api. Providers are replaceable implementations; the shared mail model and safety policy are the product.

title: Author the minimal canonical policy fragments
description:
Why: machine-state-9tw.4 cannot write manifests with no sources to point at, and no bead ever created canonical policy content. The original reconciliation bead was withdrawn once machine-state-9tw.2 proved CLAUDE.md and AGENTS.md are 100 percent bd-generated, and nothing took its place. This is that gap.

SCOPE BOUNDARY, deliberate: this bead authors only SUBSTRATE-MECHANICAL content — facts about how this repo works and about each harness. It does NOT author substantive operating policy (how an agent should handle git, task tracking, shell hygiene). Two reasons: that is the user's call, not the substrate's; and bd already injects its own task-tracking guidance through a vendor-owned block plus the SessionStart hook, so duplicating it in our region would create exactly the two-copies-drifting problem this substrate exists to end.

Fragments:
  canonical/policy/00-generated.md      short banner: this region is generated, edit canonical and run ms project
  canonical/policy/10-substrate.md      what machine-state is; the canonical-to-projection rule; pointer to SUBSTRATE.md
  canonical/policy/agents/claude-harness.md   Claude-specific facts
  canonical/policy/agents/codex-harness.md    Codex-specific facts

Harness fragments carry only verified facts, not preferences:
  Claude - .claude/settings.json runs bd prime at SessionStart, so beads context arrives without asking; the harness ephemeral task tools are named TodoWrite and TaskCreate; neutral skills are linked into ~/.claude/skills.
  Codex  - no SessionStart injection here, so bd prime must be run explicitly; the beads skill lives at .agents/skills/beads/SKILL.md; Codex 0.129.0+ has native hooks, inspected with /hooks.

- Content is factual and verifiable; no invented preferences.
- No duplication of anything bd's own managed block already states.
- Combined spliced region stays well under one screen.

Plus canonical/skills/machine-state/SKILL.md (40 lines), which was not in the original bead but is required — the link target in machine-state-9tw.4 needs a skill to point at, and 'own the smallest region' forbids linking the ~/.claude/skills container instead.

Held to the scope boundary: everything authored is either a fact about this repo or a verified fact about a harness. No operating preferences invented; none of bd's own guidance duplicated. Substantive policy is deferred to machine-state-sd8.

title: Projector orphans targets removed from a manifest
description:
Found immediately after machine-state-9tw.3 closed, while verifying hash stability.

Remove a target from an adapters/*.toml and run ms project: the projected file stays on disk, its record stays in state/projection.json, and neither ms status nor ms diff mentions it. It becomes state nobody tracks. Retargeting an adapter therefore silently leaves the old projection behind, which undermines both the drift model and the promise in SUBSTRATE.md section 8 that the substrate can be cleanly removed.

Fix: treat a record whose key no target claims as an ORPHAN.
- ms project reconciles: removes the orphan and drops its record.
- ms status and ms diff report orphans rather than ignoring them.
- Removal must be conservative. A render orphan is deleted only if its bytes still match the recorded sha; if a human has since edited it, leave it in place and say so. splice orphans lose only our marker region. link orphans are just a symlink.

Reproduced 2026-08-31 in a scratch copy: dropped a link target from the manifest, projected, and linkdest remained on disk with its record intact and no command reporting it.
acceptance_criteria:
- Removing a target from a manifest and running ms project removes the projection and its record.
- ms status and ms diff name orphans explicitly.
- A render orphan whose content was edited after projection is NOT deleted; it is reported and left alone.
- unproject uses the same conservative removal path.
notes:
FIXED 2026-08-31. Added orphans() plus a shared remove_recorded() used by both project reconciliation and unproject, so the two can never diverge in how carefully they remove things.

Conservative removal by kind: link unlinks a symlink; splice removes only our marker region; render deletes ONLY if the bytes still match the recorded sha, otherwise reports 'edited since we wrote it; left in place' and keeps the file.

VERIFIED: dropping a target from a manifest now shows as orphan in diff (exit 1) and status, and ms project removes it and clears the record. An edited render orphan survives both project and unproject. Full regression after the change: idempotent and hash-stable over three runs, diff clean exit 0, link still a symlink, splice round-trip byte-identical, unproject leaves nothing, vendor render still refused, no temp files.
close_reason: Orphan reconciliation implemented and verified, with conservative removal that never deletes a file edited after projection.

title: Decide DCG safety posture: fail-open default, 3 of 103 packs, no config file
description:
Why: dcg is designated the safety boundary beneath all agent harnesses, but its installed posture is entirely built-in defaults and nobody has yet decided whether those defaults are the intended policy. 'dcg doctor' passes — but passing means 'correctly installed', not 'configured as we intend'.

OBSERVED 2026-08-31 (dcg 0.13.9, all read-only checks):

1. NO CONFIG FILE AT ANY LAYER. dcg doctor reports 'USING DEFAULTS'.
     system  /etc/dcg/config.toml            missing (full)
     user    ~/.config/dcg/config.toml       missing (full)
     project /home/klaas/src/machine-state/.dcg.toml   missing (enforcement-only)

2. FAIL-OPEN. 'Fail closed: false'. On unparseable hook input dcg ALLOWS the command. For a
   component whose stated role is a safety boundary, defaulting to allow on confusion is a
   posture worth deciding deliberately rather than inheriting. DCG_FAIL_CLOSED=1 flips it.

3. THREE OF 103 PACKS ENABLED: core.filesystem, core.git, system.disk. Everything else is off,
   including the egress and guardrail-tampering families. Empirically core.filesystem works —
   it blocked an rm -rf during this session.

4. WIRED FOR ONE HARNESS. The dcg hook exists only in ~/.claude/settings.json (user-global,
   PreToolUse). Nothing is broken today, because Claude is the only supported harness installed.
   But the stated intent is that dcg applies REGARDLESS of which agent operates, and wiring a
   newly installed harness is a separate manual 'dcg install' step. Intent is currently
   satisfiable but unverified for any future harness.

5. NO ALLOWLIST ENTRIES. Hook self-heal on, evaluation budget 1000 ms.

DECISIONS REQUIRED:
  a. Fail-open or fail-closed?
  b. Which pack set is the intended baseline for this machine?
  c. Does the intended posture live in a user config (~/.config/dcg/config.toml, full control)
     or a project .dcg.toml (enforcement-only, and therefore projectable by machine-state)?
  d. Should ms status FAIL when a supported harness is installed but not dcg-wired?

Out of scope for substrate v0.01: this is safety policy content, not substrate plumbing. Filed
standalone so it stays visible rather than bloating the v0.01 epic.
design:
(c) is the interesting one for the substrate. A project-level .dcg.toml is enforcement-only — it can tighten but not loosen — which makes it safe to project from canonical: a projected file that can only ever increase restriction cannot become an attack on the safety boundary. A user-level config has full control and therefore should NOT be projected without more thought.

(d) is where the 'applies regardless of harness' intent becomes testable rather than aspirational: the check is per-harness, not global. Answering yes turns a manual install step into a verified invariant.
acceptance_criteria:
- Each of (a)-(d) answered and recorded.
- If a config file is adopted, its intended contents are recorded in canonical/tooling/dcg.md Intent, and dcg doctor still passes afterwards.
- No change to dcg configuration is made before the decision is recorded.
notes:
Discovered while writing the canonical tooling record in machine-state-9tw.6. Verification command for all of the above: 'dcg doctor', 'dcg config', 'dcg packs'.

APPLIED 2026-08-31, partially. ~/.config/dcg/config.toml now exists (64 lines); dcg doctor reports all checks passed with the user config loaded and 7 packs enabled.

ANSWERED:
(a) fail-open -> FAIL-CLOSED. A fail-open bypass is silent; a fail-closed error is loud and recoverable. Note: fail_closed IS a valid [general] config key even though 'dcg init' does not document it; the DCG_FAIL_CLOSED env var did not show up in 'dcg config', so the config file is the reliable path.
(b) packs -> enable by INSTALLED SURFACE. Added package_managers, system.services, system.permissions, secret_disclosure, matching pacman, uwsm-managed systemd user units, HOME, and private keys. Cloud/kubernetes/containers/database/infrastructure/windows/cicd stay off; rules for absent software protect nothing and only misfire. Correction to an earlier claim: the previous '3 of 103' was not a choice at all — core is always on and cannot be disabled, and system.disk is on by default.
(c) layer -> USER config, hand-applied, NOT projected. That layer can loosen as well as tighten, so projecting it would let a bad edit in canonical/ silently weaken the boundary. A project .dcg.toml is enforcement-only and would be safe to project if per-repo tightening is ever wanted.

ALSO: observability was off entirely — no log file, and history disabled, so 'dcg history analyze' was reading an empty database and recommending that core be disabled for inactivity on the same day core blocked two real commands. Both now enabled; history recording confirmed working.

STAGED ROLLOUT: the four new packs are set to 'warn' in [policy.packs] while core and system.disk keep denying. Verified empirically — a package_managers pattern returns 'WARN (policy allows)' while core.git force-push returns 'BLOCKED'. Note that [policy.packs] modes are NOT visible in 'dcg config' output; 'dcg test' against a matching pattern is the only way to confirm a pack's mode.

STILL OPEN, which is why this bead stays open:
- Promote the four packs from warn to deny once the log shows what they match. Give it a week of normal work. Removing those four lines is the last step of this decision, not a new one.
- (d) whether ms status should fail when an installed harness is not dcg-wired. Needs a projector change, not config.

(d) ANSWERED AND IMPLEMENTED 2026-09-01. Yes, ms status now fails when an installed harness is not covered by the guard.

Design: harness records may declare an optional 'wiring' command. Present but unwired prints ** UNGUARDED ** and makes ms status exit non-zero. Absent harnesses are skipped — what is not installed cannot be unguarded, so Codex raises no false alarm. state/tooling.json records a 'guarded' boolean alongside the version.

Verified by negative control, not just by passing: pointing DCG_CONFIG at a nonexistent file makes the wiring check fail, claude reports UNGUARDED, and ms status exits 1. Restoring it returns exit 0.

LATENT BUG FOUND AND FIXED IN ALREADY-SHIPPED WORK: plain 'dcg doctor' exits 0 EVEN WHEN ITS CHECKS FAIL; only --strict signals through the exit code. The dcg record was using plain 'dcg doctor', so the Safety line could never have reported a problem — it would have shown 'active' with the guard broken. Now 'dcg doctor --strict', and the negative control shows 'degraded' correctly. A tooling record that looked green for the wrong reason is precisely the failure these records exist to prevent.

CODEX GAP RECORDED, NOT FAKED: dcg install has flags for Claude, Grok, agy, OpenCode and omp but NONE for Codex, and dcg doctor only inspects Claude's hook registration. Nothing can currently prove Codex would be guarded. codex.md declares no wiring key and says why, and states that establishing wiring is part of installing Codex rather than an afterthought.

The two lines answer different questions — is the guard healthy, versus is THIS HARNESS guarded — and will diverge as soon as a second harness exists. Documented so it is not later 'cleaned up' as duplication.
